body: Production migrations roll forward, never back. Backwards migrations exist in the tree and get used freely on laptops, but running one against production is treated as an incident action requiring a second engineer in the channel. That standing decision came out of the night someone reversed a column rename using the generated down step and lost four hours of shipment status writes, because the reverse of a rename that already has traffic on it is not a rename. What replaced rollback is expand/contract. Every schema change ships as an additive migration first, and the destructive half — dropping the old column, tightening the constraint — lands in a separate release at least one deploy later, so the running application is always compatible with both the previous and the next schema. `make migrate-check` runs `tools/migration_guard.py` in the pipeline and fails on DROP COLUMN, type alterations against populated tables, and index creation without CONCURRENTLY, unless the migration carries an explicit `reviewed_destructive = true` marker with a linked ticket. When a change genuinely has to be undone in production, the answer is a new hand-written forward migration reviewed by two people. Point-in-time restore is the last resort and is a full cluster restore, so it costs the whole database rather than one table. The planning consequence: any schema change needing a cleanup pass is two tickets from the start, not one.

Flag cleanup is enforced by the build, not by good intentions. Every flag is declared in `config/flags.yaml` with an owner, a ticket and a required `expires_on` date no more than ninety days out, and the loader refuses to boot if a flag is referenced in code but missing from that file. A nightly workflow runs `python -m tools.flag_audit`, which fails for any flag past its expiry with no open removal PR and posts the list into the owning team's channel. Removal is two deploys, always in the same order: flip the default in the config and ship it, let it sit through one full release cycle so reverting is still cheap, then delete the branches in code and drop the row from `feature_flags`. Skipping that wait is what produced the invoicing outage. A kill switch nobody had touched in two years was still wired into the settlement path, and someone tidying stale entries in the admin UI toggled it off mid-afternoon. That was the second incident traced to an abandoned flag, which is the point at which cleanup stopped being hygiene and became a gate. The heuristic that came out of the review: a flag whose expiry has been extended twice is not a flag, it is configuration, and it should either be promoted to a real setting or deleted outright.

The nightly backup job used to count as green if the snapshot API call returned zero. That belief cost us when WAL archiving broke silently for eleven days — snapshots were being taken, the dashboard stayed green, and the point-in-time recovery window we thought we had did not exist. Nobody noticed until an engineer tried to recover a dropped table and found the earliest restorable point was the previous week.

Since then, a backup is not considered taken until it has been restored. `ops/backup/verify_restore.sh` runs at 04:10 UTC, provisions a throwaway instance from the most recent automated snapshot, replays WAL to the newest available LSN, then runs three checks: `pg_restore --list` against the logical dump to confirm it parses, a row-count comparison on `shipments` and `tariff_versions` against production within a tolerance band, and a checksum over the previous day's closed ledger entries. The instance is destroyed at the end regardless of outcome.

The job emits `backup_restore_verified_age_seconds`, and the page fires when that exceeds 26 hours. The alert is deliberately on the verification's age, not the snapshot's — that distinction is the entire point of the rebuild. Do not silence it by re-running the snapshot; the snapshot was never the thing in doubt.

What the runbook says and what actually happens differ, and the difference is intentional. Written policy is: primary pages, fifteen minutes to auto-escalate to secondary, then the engineering manager. In practice the secondary is almost never paged by the tool — the primary opens the incident channel and pulls in whoever owns the failing service, and that person joins voluntarily, usually within a couple of minutes. Manager escalation is reserved for decisions that are not technical: getting a vendor's account team on the phone at night, deciding to accept data loss, deciding to wake an executive. The norms that came out of the bad night in spring and have held since: the primary's job is to declare, not to fix — nobody has ever been criticised for declaring early, and a few people have been criticised for waiting. Anyone can raise a severity; only the incident commander can lower it. Customer-facing comms go out at the thirty-minute mark whether or not there is a diagnosis, because during that outage the silence generated more inbound support volume than the outage did. And the schedule is authoritative for paging but not for reality — people swap shifts by saying so in the channel and often never update the tool, so when it matters who is actually awake, ask in the channel instead of trusting the rotation view.

Public API rate limiting lives at the edge gateway, not in the application, and is keyed on the API key rather than the source IP — customer integrations run behind NAT and shared egress, so IP buckets punished the wrong callers. Token bucket per key: `sustained_rate = 20` requests per second with `burst = 60`, configured in `services/gateway/ratelimit.yaml` and hot-reloaded without a deploy.

Those numbers came from measuring the p99 request rate of legitimate nightly batch jobs across the top twenty accounts and rounding up roughly 3x. They are not a capacity limit — the gateway saturates far above them — they are an abuse and runaway-loop limit, which is why raising one is routine rather than fraught.

Two carve-outs. The webhook replay endpoint gets its own much tighter bucket, because a customer retry storm there fans out into ledger writes. All sandbox keys share a single global bucket on purpose, so load testing against sandbox can never be mistaken for a production signal.

Rejected requests return 429 with Retry-After, and remaining budget is exposed on every response so integrators can pace themselves instead of discovering the wall.

Raising a ceiling is a config change plus a look at the gateway saturation panel first. We have never refused one, but twice the customer's real problem turned out to be polling a list endpoint instead of consuming webhooks, and we fixed that instead.

Decided in March and now the rule for everything on the cluster: application secrets arrive as files, never as environment variables. The external-secrets operator in the `platform-system` namespace reconciles one `ExternalSecret` per service against AWS Secrets Manager under `/kestrel/<env>/<service>/`, writes a native Kubernetes Secret, and the service's Helm chart mounts it as a projected volume at `/var/run/secrets/kestrel/`. Services read the file at point of use instead of caching it at boot, so a rotation propagates within the operator's `refreshInterval: 15m` with no rollout — that was the whole point of the migration, since the old pattern required a full redeploy to rotate anything and so nobody rotated. Env vars were rejected on specifics, not taste: they are inherited by every forked child, readable out of /proc by anything sharing the pid namespace, and we found database passwords verbatim in crash-reporter payloads twice last year. Second reason, and the one to cite when someone proposes a shared "app secrets" bundle again: each pod's service account assumes an IAM role scoped to its own prefix, so a compromised container cannot read another service's material. One exception still stands — the legacy invoicer reads its database password once during Rails initialisation, so it is injected at boot and rotating it there still means a restart. That exception disappears with the billing cutover, not before.

The review agreement, made at the retro after a quarter where the median pull request sat almost four days, is about first response and nothing else: a reviewer acknowledges within one business day, either taking it or handing it to someone who can. Acknowledgement is explicitly not approval, and the team deliberately refused to turn this into a measured SLA. The earlier dashboard experiment produced fast approvals with no comments inside them, which everyone agreed was worse than slow ones. Small changes, roughly under two hundred lines, are expected the same day. Large refactors are supposed to be arranged with a named reviewer before the branch opens, so nobody meets a two-thousand-line diff cold and then quietly avoids it for a week. Urgent production fixes skip blocking review entirely: pair with whoever is oncall, merge, review after the fact. The part that mattered most in practice turned out to be social rather than procedural. The author pings the channel once, and after that it is the reviewer's problem and not the author's, so chasing stopped feeling rude and people stopped accumulating stacks of dependent branches out of politeness.

Background jobs are named `domain.verb_object`, lowercase snake_case on both sides of the dot: `billing.retry_failed_charge`, `ledger.close_daily_period`, `notifications.send_invoice_email`. No `_job` or `_task` suffix — the registry already tells you what kind of thing it is. The domain segment is not decorative: the queue a job lands on is derived from it, so mislabeling the domain silently routes work to the wrong worker pool and the wrong alert route.

The pattern is enforced by a test that walks every key in `services/worker/registry.py` and matches it against the regex, so a badly named job fails CI instead of relying on someone catching it in review.

Treat a rename as a breaking change. Queued messages carry the job name as a plain string, so a deploy that renames without an alias will find in-flight messages with no handler and dead-letter them. The procedure is: register the new name, keep the old one as an alias for one full release, delete it once the queue has drained past the retention window.

The convention came out of an incident where two teams owned jobs whose names differed only by pluralization, and the on-call engineer paused the wrong one while working a backlog. A job name should tell you which team owns it and what it does to what, without opening the code.

The agreed shape of the invoicer retirement, out of the planning session with finance: dual-write first, then shadow reads, then per-tenant read flips, then a long read-only tail. No step skipped, and no date attached to any of them. Dual-write has to survive at least one full month-end close before anything else moves, because the rare proration and mid-cycle plan-change paths only execute at close; a week of weekday traffic proves nearly nothing about the code paths that are expensive when wrong. During shadow reads the diff report is the deliverable, not the migration itself — legacy stays authoritative, the new service computes in parallel, and every discrepancy gets explained rather than tuned away, because the legacy rounding behaviour is baked into signed contracts and "the new number is more correct" is not a defence anyone can take to a customer. Read flips go smallest tenant first, and finance holds the go/no-go, not engineering; their bar is two consecutive closes with an empty diff across the top revenue tier. Two standing constraints: no schema changes to the legacy database while parallel running is on, so that any diff is attributable; and rollback means pointing reads back at legacy, which only works while dual-write is still running. The day writes stop is the real point of no return — after that, rollback is a restore. The whole thing is gated on empty diffs rather than a date because date pressure on the last migration is exactly what produced the shortcuts we are still paying for.

We stopped using the monorepo in the spring, about eighteen months after adopting it. The reason was not a technical failure of the tooling — it was that the feedback signal had gone dead. With twenty engineers committing into one tree and no build graph, every pull request ran the full test matrix, which drifted from six minutes to over forty. People stopped reading CI results and started merging on the assumption that whatever was red belonged to somebody else's flake. That state is exactly what we had adopted the monorepo to avoid.

The alternative we weighed first was keeping the single tree and buying honest incrementality with a build-graph tool. We rejected it deliberately. A correct build graph is a standing maintenance obligation, and we have no platform team to carry it; choosing it would have meant one senior engineer permanently assigned to build infrastructure, which is a worse trade than the one we made.

So the tree was split into one repository per deployable service, with the shared domain models extracted into an internal library published as a versioned package. We went in with eyes open on the costs: cross-cutting changes now need coordinated pull requests in three or four places, version skew between services is possible and will eventually bite us, and atomic refactors across service boundaries are gone. Those are visible, occasional costs. A CI signal nobody trusts is an invisible, continuous one.

Adding a runtime dependency requires a written case in the pull request. Adding a development or test dependency does not. The case has to answer three things: what specifically breaks if we write the needed slice ourselves, who maintains the package upstream and how recently they shipped, and what removing it later would cost. Reviewers push hardest on the first question, because most proposed dependencies are being pulled in for a small fraction of what they actually do.

Anything touching money arithmetic, authentication, or the serialization of stored records needs two approvals instead of one. Those are the places where a quiet upstream behaviour change becomes a correctness bug that our tests will happily go green on.

The policy is deliberately not about install size or build time. Both come up in review and neither has ever blocked a change. It exists because a runtime dependency is a standing trust decision and an ongoing patching obligation, and the expensive moment is never the day you add it — it is two years later, discovering that an unmaintained package sits underneath the billing path and nobody remembers what it was chosen over. Vendoring a hundred lines with a comment recording where they came from is an accepted outcome and often the preferred one.

Retention on the self-hosted log stack is fourteen days and that is deliberate, not a leftover default. It was set during the storage review after the object-store bill for the logging cluster passed the compute bill for the entire staging environment; at ninety days of ingest the index alone was the third-largest line item and growing with traffic, while the query telemetry showed almost nothing reaching past six days. The second reason is the one that actually locks it in place: request logs carry shipper names, pickup addresses and partial consignment numbers, and the data-handling policy caps identifiable transit data at two weeks unless it passes through redaction. Nobody had the appetite to build and own a redaction pipeline purely so debug logs could live longer, so the shorter window answered both problems at once. Long-lived evidence lives elsewhere by design. The financial audit trail is a separate append-only store kept for seven years, and metrics and traces are downsampled and held for thirteen months, which covered both of the incidents where anyone genuinely needed older history. Standing guidance for whoever is oncall is to export the relevant window to the incident archive bucket while they are still responding, rather than asking to raise the global retention afterwards. That request has come up three times and been declined three times.

Force-pushing a shared branch is prohibited, and the rule dates from the afternoon `release/2409` lost three merged pull requests: someone rebased to tidy their own commits, did not notice their local ref was two days stale, and pushed over the branch. The reflog that saved us lived on exactly one laptop, and recovery ate an afternoon of a release freeze.

Force-push freely on branches nobody else has touched — your own `feat/*` work before review — and always with `--force-with-lease` rather than `--force`, because the lease turns losing a race into a rejected push instead of a silent overwrite. Never on `main`, anything under `release/*`, or a branch with an open pull request someone else has reviewed or built on. If shared history genuinely needs rewriting, open a new branch and a fresh PR rather than doing surgery in place.

Enforcement is doubled on purpose, because the policy alone did not hold: branch protection rejects non-fast-forward pushes to the protected patterns, and `.githooks/pre-push` catches the obvious cases before the network is touched. The hook only fires in clones that set `core.hooksPath`, which the bootstrap script does. The remote rule is the guarantee; the hook exists so the failure is fast and legible.

`ClientDisconnect` is filtered out of error tracking on purpose — the `before_send` hook in `services/api/observability.py` drops it before anything leaves the process. It is raised by the ASGI server whenever a caller hangs up mid-response, which for us means mobile clients on poor networks and load balancer probes timing out at an awkward moment. Nothing in that path is actionable: the request is already gone, and no state is left half-written because the transaction boundary closes before the response starts streaming.

The reason this is worth recording is volume. Before the filter it was roughly two thirds of all reported events, which pushed genuine regressions off the first page of the issue list and consumed the monthly event quota by about the third week.

Dropping it from error tracking is not dropping it from observability. The same exception still increments `http_client_disconnect_total`, and a sustained spike there is a real signal — usually an upstream proxy whose idle timeout is shorter than ours, which is exactly how the misconfigured edge timeout was found last winter.

There was a proposal to add `TimeoutError` to the same ignore list because it is also noisy. Rejected: those are our timeouts against our own dependencies, and they are precisely the thing we want to be woken up about.

The integration suite runs on a single worker deliberately: `make test-integration` shells out to `pytest tests/integration -n 0`, and CI passes the same flag. This is not an oversight and should not be "fixed" by turning workers back on. Every integration test shares one Postgres database, and the session fixture truncates all tables between tests; under xdist, one worker's truncation deleted rows another worker was mid-assertion on, which surfaced as roughly a four percent flake rate that people handled by re-running until green. That habit costs more than the eight minutes serial execution costs. Per-worker schemas were tried and abandoned — the rating engine resolves tenants through a materialised view whose refresh trigger hardcodes `public`, and two migrations install database-scoped extension objects that cannot be duplicated per schema. Doing it properly means making the search path configurable inside the rating engine, which is worth doing eventually and not worth doing to reclaim eight minutes of wall clock. Unit tests still run fully parallel; the serial constraint applies only to the database-backed suite.

Moved connection pooling out of the application processes and into a standalone PgBouncer deployment in September, after the second connection-exhaustion incident in a month. The app-side pools were the problem: each `dispatch-api` pod opened its own pool of 20, and the HPA happily scaled to 60 pods during the pre-holiday tender surge, so we asked for roughly 1200 backends against an RDS instance with `max_connections = 500`. Postgres does not degrade gracefully there — it refuses, the refusals landed on the healthcheck path, pods got killed, and the survivors scaled harder into the same wall.

PgBouncer now runs as its own deployment behind a ClusterIP service with `pool_mode = transaction` and a server pool sized to 180. Application pools were cut to 2 per process, which keeps latency flat because the client-side pool is now only absorbing thread contention, not connection setup.

The cost is real and worth naming: transaction pooling means no session state survives a statement boundary. We moved LISTEN/NOTIFY in the `ledger` worker onto a direct connection that bypasses the pooler, dropped server-side prepared statements in the Go services, and audited every `SET LOCAL` we depended on. Session-scoped advisory locks were rewritten as row locks. Anything that genuinely needs a session gets a documented direct-connect DSN — never a per-service exception carved into the pooler config.

The frontend build output is intentionally not cached in CI, and there is a comment saying so in `.github/workflows/web-ci.yml` because two different people have since tried to add it back. We cached the Vite output and `node_modules` for about three weeks in early spring and spent most of that time chasing ghosts. The cache key was the lockfile hash alone, but the bundle embeds the commit SHA and the API client generated from the schema at build time, so a fully green pipeline could ship chunks built against last week's types. Two of those reached production before anyone connected the symptoms to the cache. The payoff was small even when it behaved: cold build measured around 3m10s against 2m40s warm once the runners moved to the larger instance class, and restoring a 400 MB directory over the network ate most of that difference. What stayed is the package store cache keyed on `pnpm-lock.yaml`, which is content-addressed and cannot go stale the same way. If build time becomes painful again, the agreed direction is to split the CI job per workspace package and parallelise, not to reintroduce an output cache.

Staging runs against a single shared database on purpose; it is not an accident of neglect. We started with ephemeral per-branch databases seeded from fixtures. Two problems killed that: seeding a realistic freight dataset took most of half an hour, so people skipped staging entirely, and the fixtures slowly diverged from the shapes real customers produce. The bugs that actually reached production were almost never logic bugs the fixtures would have caught — they were data-shape bugs. The multi-leg shipment with a null intermediate stop. The tariff with an open-ended validity window. Synthetic seed data never had those.

Staging now points at one long-lived database restored weekly from a scrubbed production dump, and everyone shares it. We took the contention knowingly: engineers occasionally stomp each other's test records, migrations have to be sequenced rather than applied in parallel, and destructive tests are banned there — those belong on a local instance.

The framing that keeps this from becoming a mess is that staging is not a correctness gate. CI is the correctness gate, and CI still uses isolated per-run databases with fixtures. Staging answers one narrower question: does this behave sanely against data that looks like the real thing. Because that is its only job, one shared database is sufficient, and the fidelity of real-shaped data is worth more to us than isolation would be.

Every Dockerfile pins its base by digest — `FROM public.ecr.aws/docker/library/python:3.12-slim@sha256:<digest>` — and `scripts/check_base_digests.py` runs in the lint job, failing any FROM line without an `@sha256:` suffix. The reason is one specific outage: upstream retagged the slim image with a newer glibc, our tag-only pin silently picked it up during an unrelated rebuild, and the ledger service began segfaulting inside a compiled dependency in production six hours after an identical-looking build had passed staging. Tags are mutable, so a tag pin only means the artifact you tested and the artifact you shipped are probably the same image. A digest makes rebuilds reproducible and turns a base upgrade into a reviewed one-line diff with a changelog attached, rather than something that happens to you. Second reason, added later: the release gate matches the build attestation against the base digest, so an unpinned FROM breaks provenance verification outright. Maintenance cost stays low because the dependency bot opens the digest bump weekly — pinning buys determinism at the price of merging a PR, not at the price of vigilance.

Retired the shared development host in the second quarter and moved everyone to per-developer environments. The trigger was a half-applied schema migration that one engineer ran against the shared database on a Tuesday morning and left the entire backend team unable to boot the app until late afternoon; that was the third outage of the same class in a year. The deeper argument, and the one that actually settled it, is that a shared box makes every developer's environment a piece of production-shaped infrastructure nobody owns: it drifts from what is deployed, it accumulates hand-applied fixes that live in no repository, and it turns cheap local experiments into changes with a blast radius.

Someone proposed provisioning a second host so teams could split across them. We rejected that because capacity was never the constraint — shared mutable state was, and two hosts halve the pain rather than remove it.

The tradeoffs were accepted knowingly. Laptops are slower for the full integration stack, first-day setup takes longer, and a few people lost the convenience of a machine that was always warm. In exchange, a broken environment is now one person's problem and is fixed by throwing it away rather than by asking in chat whether anyone else is mid-migration. If reviving a shared box comes up again for cost reasons, the answer is no on isolation grounds, not on cost.

Alongside the physical backups, a nightly `pg_dump -Fc` of the `config` database is taken and kept for thirty days. It is small, about forty megabytes, and it exists for a restore granularity the physical chain cannot offer. Physical backups restore a cluster; when someone truncates the feature flag definitions or a bad migration rewrites the tariff band table, restoring a cluster to recover one table means either rolling back everything else or standing up a scratch instance from the archive first, which is an hour of work under pressure. A custom-format dump can be restored table by table into the live database with one command, turning that hour into a few minutes. The dump is deliberately limited to `config`; the same reasoning applied to the booking tables would produce something too large and too far behind to be useful, and the temptation to extend it should be resisted. It is written to the same bucket under its own prefix with its own lifecycle rule. It substitutes for nothing — the physical chain remains the recovery path of record, and this exists only for surgical repair of small, slowly-changing reference data.

We put a merge queue in front of the trunk and dropped the ritual of updating your branch immediately before merging. The ritual never actually worked: it proved your branch was green against the trunk as of a few minutes ago, which says nothing once two people merge in the same window, and it created a race where whoever landed second had to redo the whole dance. The trunk was broken about twice a week, almost always by a semantic conflict — two changes that each pass alone and fail together, typically a renamed field and a new caller of the old name. The queue batches up to five pull requests, tests the combined result, and bisects the batch on failure so the guilty change is ejected instead of the whole group. Median time from approval to merge rose by roughly eight minutes, which people noticed and grumbled about, and broken-trunk incidents fell to about one a month, which they noticed less because nothing happened. We took the trade because a broken trunk blocks everyone while a slower merge blocks one person.

Audit events are not logs and do not travel through the logging pipeline. Anything recording who changed what — permission grants, refunds issued, customer data exports, production config edits — is written to a dedicated append-only store with object lock enabled and a seven-year policy, because that is what our payments licence requires and what an auditor will ask to see.

Separating the two was the first thing we did after the first compliance review, and the reason is that they have opposite requirements. Operational telemetry wants to be cheap, high-volume, queryable in seconds, and disposable. Audit records want to be low-volume, tamper-evident, provably complete, and expensive to destroy. Serving both from one system meant either paying operational-scale storage costs for compliance-grade durability, or quietly failing an audit because the evidence had aged out of a system that was never designed to hold it.

The write path differs too, deliberately. Audit writes are synchronous, and a failure to write is a failure of the operation itself — a refund that cannot be recorded does not happen. Operational logging is fire-and-forget and drops under pressure, which is exactly correct for one of them and completely unacceptable for the other.

The repository ruleset in `.github/rulesets/main.json` sets `require_last_push_approval = true` and disables admin bypass for everyone except the release automation account. The first setting closes a hole we walked into: an author pushed a rebase after receiving approval, the approval carried over, and a conflict resolution that silently dropped a validation check merged with a green review attached to different code. Nobody did anything wrong procedurally, which is exactly why it needed a mechanical fix rather than a reminder. Removing admin bypass was the more contentious half, since a handful of people had been using it to unstick merges when a flaky check would not go green. That is a real problem, but the answer is fixing the flaky check, and leaving the bypass in place removed the pressure to ever do so. The release account keeps its exemption because tag and changelog commits are generated from an already-reviewed state, and that exemption is scoped by path so it cannot touch application code.

Data backfills run through `scripts/backfill_runner.py` as ordinary jobs, never inside a schema revision. The runner reads `BACKFILL_BATCH_SIZE = 5000`, commits each batch, sleeps briefly between them, and records its cursor in a `backfill_progress` table keyed by job name and last processed id. That structure gives three properties we needed. It is resumable, so a runner killed halfway through picks up where it stopped instead of starting over on forty million rows. It is pausable, so an on-call engineer can stop it during an incident without rolling anything back. And it never holds a transaction open longer than one batch, which keeps replication lag bounded and stops the backfill from blocking ordinary writes. Every backfill must be written so that running it twice is harmless, because in practice every long backfill is run more than once — interrupted deploys, a bad batch size, a widened predicate. Idempotence is checked in review by asking what happens on a second pass, and a job that cannot answer that does not merge.

The encryption key for the backup bucket is held in a different account from the one that can delete objects in it, and no operator has both. The threat this addresses is not really an outside attacker but a single compromised or mistaken administrator: separating custody means destroying the backups requires two independent things to go wrong. Changes to the key policy need approval from two named people, and the approval is on the change itself rather than standing. The cost is real and was accepted with eyes open — a restore needs an explicit cross-account grant, which adds a step and several minutes to recovery and cannot be done by whoever is on call alone. That trade was deliberate: the scenario where minutes matter is losing the primary, and that is served by the local snapshots, not by the encrypted archive. Rotation is annual and the retired key is retained rather than destroyed, because a key destroyed on schedule takes every backup encrypted under it with it. That last point took a while to argue and is the part most likely to be quietly undone by someone tidying up.

Base backups run against `pg-standby-b`, not the primary, and a proposal to move them back to the primary for simplicity was rejected. Taking a base backup is sustained sequential read plus the checkpoint it forces, and on the primary that showed up as a doubling of write p99 for the twenty-odd minutes it ran; moving it to a standby removed the effect entirely and cost nothing, since the standby's only other job is being ready. The proposal argued that a backup from a replica can be behind, which is true and irrelevant at our lag, and that it adds a dependency on the standby being healthy, which is the real objection. That one was answered by making standby health a backup concern: if the designated standby is unavailable at backup time the job fails loudly rather than falling back, and the alert says which of the two problems it is. Silently backing up the primary instead would have been the worst outcome — the same latency incident, unexplained, at an hour nobody is watching. The job pins one named standby rather than resolving whichever is available, so the backup source is a known thing during an incident rather than something to be worked out.

Base backups were moved off the attached-volume snapshot mechanism and into object storage with a lifecycle policy. Volume snapshots were fast to take and fast to restore but were tied to the account and region that held the volume, which made the disaster scenario we actually care about — losing that account — unrecoverable. Backups now land in a bucket in a separate account, with a lifecycle rule transitioning objects older than 30 days to the infrequent-access class and expiring them at `400d`. Volume snapshots were kept but their retention was cut to three days, since their remaining job is fast recovery from a same-region mistake, not durability. The tiering saves roughly two thirds of the storage line and costs retrieval time on old restores, which is the correct trade: restores from beyond a month are compliance requests with a lead time, not incidents. One consequence was written into the runbook explicitly because it surprised us in rehearsal — retrieval from the cold class is charged per gigabyte, so pulling a full cluster from an old backup is a decision with a price attached rather than a reflex.

Branch names start with the ticket ID: `ENG-1423-invoice-rounding`. The hook at `.githooks/pre-push` enforces `^(ENG|OPS|SEC)-[0-9]+-[a-z0-9-]+$`, and CI re-checks it because hooks are opt-in and half the team clones fresh every few months. This is not about tidiness. Three separate tools parse that prefix: the deploy dashboard links a running preview environment back to its ticket, the changelog generator groups entries by epic, and the incident bot can answer "what shipped near this ticket" without a human search. Before the convention, roughly a third of branches were named after the author's guess at the problem and none of that automation was possible. The escape hatch is a `spike/` prefix for throwaway work, exempt from the pattern and also exempt from preview environments; if a spike turns into real work it is renamed before review. We considered generating the branch name from the ticket with a CLI wrapper and the team pushed back on another layer around git, and compliance has held above ninety-five percent without it.

Client-side errors from the shipper portal go to a separate tracker project from the backend services, with its own quota, its own alert routing, and its own retention. They were combined originally and it did not survive contact with the open internet. Browser events are dominated by things that are not our bugs — extensions injecting scripts, ad blockers breaking script loads, network failures on mobile, ancient browsers, and outright bot traffic — at a volume that buried backend issues in the shared views and consumed a disproportionate share of the budget. Splitting them let us set genuinely different policies. The frontend project tolerates a much lower signal-to-noise ratio and is triaged in a weekly sweep rather than alerting in real time, because almost nothing there warrants waking someone. The backend project keeps real-time alerting precisely because its baseline is quiet. The cost is that a full-stack failure now shows up in two places and someone has to correlate them, which we handle by carrying a shared request identifier in both. That has been good enough; the alternative of one project with elaborate filtering was tried first and the filters were always slightly wrong.

Build-time secrets never land in an image layer. The private package registry token is passed as `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token`, which exposes it at `/run/secrets/npm_token` for the duration of that instruction and leaves nothing behind. Before this it was a build argument, and `docker history` on any published image showed it in clear text; we found such an image in the public mirror during a routine scan and spent an afternoon rotating the token and rebuilding fourteen services. Two rules came out of that. Any credential used to fetch dependencies is scoped read-only and to a single registry path, so the worst case is a leaked read of packages we publish anyway. And the image scanner in CI fails the build on a secret pattern found in layer metadata, not only in the filesystem, because the original leak was in metadata and the scanner we had walked straight past it. Build tokens rotate monthly and are entirely separate from anything a running workload is entitled to.

Every secret read is audited, and a bulk read pages the on-call. The audit device writes to `/var/log/vault/audit.log`, shipped to the log store within a minute, and the alert fires when `vault_secret_read_total` for a single identity exceeds fifty in five minutes. Normal services sit far under that — most read a handful of paths at startup and then nothing — so the rule has fired four times in a year: twice for a misconfigured retry loop, once for a migration we now silence in advance, and once for an engineer enumerating paths to build an inventory, which is precisely the behaviour we want to see surfaced. The threshold is per identity rather than global, because a global one is drowned by deploy waves and would have been turned off inside a week. We keep the audit log for two years, longer than general log retention, because the question it answers — who could have seen this before we rotated it — is only ever asked months later. The audit device fails closed.

The size check in `.github/workflows/size.yml` downloads `dist/stats.json` from the most recent successful main run and compares the pull request's bundle against that, instead of building main a second time inside the PR job. Rebuilding doubled the job's cost and, worse, made the comparison nondeterministic: a floating transitive dependency could move the baseline between two runs of an unchanged branch, so the reported delta wandered by tens of kilobytes with no source change and people learned to ignore the check entirely. Pinning the baseline to a specific commit, named in the check output, makes a regression attributable to a diff someone can read. The budget fails hard at a fifteen-kilobyte gzip increase on the entry chunk and warns below that. If main has no green run in the last thirty days the check reports neutral rather than failing, because a silently stale baseline is worse than no baseline and a red check nobody trusts is worse than both.

CI dependency caches are keyed on a hash of the lockfile rather than on the branch name. The old key was the branch, which meant a long-lived feature branch kept serving a cache built weeks earlier and two builds of the same commit could resolve different transitive versions depending on which runner picked them up. We chased a test that only failed on one branch for two days before understanding it was a stale wheel. The key is now `deps-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/uv.lock') }}` with a prefix restore key, so an unchanged-but-not-identical dependency set still gets a warm start instead of a cold install. Cache entries are immutable once written; nothing overwrites a key. Median install time fell from just over six minutes to under forty seconds on a hit, and more importantly a green build on a branch now means the same dependency graph the merge will use. The same pattern was applied to the frontend and to the container base layer. The rule generalises: a cache key must be derived from the content that determines the cached artifact, never from a name that happens to be nearby.

A CI job runs `alembic heads` and fails unless it prints exactly one line. Two branches each adding a revision off the same parent produce two heads, and `upgrade head` then becomes ambiguous — we found this in staging when a deploy applied one of two expected changes and reported success, and the missing table was not noticed for a day. The resolution policy is to rebase the later branch and repoint its `down_revision` at the other's identifier, rather than reaching for `alembic merge`. A merge revision is legitimate tooling but it preserves a fork in the history, and six months later nobody reading the graph can tell what order things actually applied in. Merge revisions are permitted only when both branches have already shipped to production and rebasing would rewrite applied history, which has happened twice. The check runs on pull requests rather than at deploy time on purpose, because the person who can cheaply fix a second head is the author of the second branch, on the day they wrote it.

Production images do not run a resolver. The build step exports the locked tree with `uv export --format requirements-txt --generate-hashes > requirements.lock` and the Dockerfile installs with `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.lock`. Any artifact whose digest does not match the lock aborts the build. This came out of a near-miss where a registry mirror served a rebuilt wheel with a different digest for an already-released version; nothing malicious was found, but nothing in our pipeline would have noticed either. Hash-pinning turns that class of event from invisible into a hard build failure. The cost is real and we chose to pay it: the export step adds about forty seconds to every image build, and platform-specific wheels mean the lock has to be exported per target architecture, which is why `ops/build/export-locks.sh` loops over the two we ship. Local development is exempt and still uses the resolver directly, because forcing hash mode on laptops made every casual experiment painful for no security benefit. The invariant that matters is narrow: nothing reaches a production image without a hash that was reviewed in a PR.

The build pool moved from hosted runners to self-hosted instances with local NVMe scratch disks. The frontend jobs were IO-bound rather than CPU-bound: dependency install writes tens of thousands of small files, and on network-attached storage that cost dominated everything else we had been tuning. Wall clock on the console pipeline fell by roughly forty percent at the same core count, which was more than any parallelism work had produced. The price is operational. Every job gets a fresh instance that is destroyed afterwards, because a reused runner is a shared mutable environment and we would rather pay boot time than debug a build that only fails on the one machine that ran a different branch an hour earlier. The pool autoscales on queue depth with a floor of two warm instances during working hours, since the cold start on the first pull request of the morning is the one people actually notice and complain about. Pull requests from forks never touch this pool; they are routed back to hosted runners, because a self-hosted runner executing workflow code from an untrusted branch is a direct path into the private network.

`/infra/` and `/deploy/` in the platform repo are owned by `@aldercross/platform-sre` in `.github/CODEOWNERS`, and branch protection requires an owner approval before merge. Product teams found this annoying for the first month, mostly on the pattern of a service needing one more environment variable in its manifest. We kept it because the two worst outages of the previous year both traced to a Terraform change reviewed only by the person who wrote it: one dropped a security group rule, the other recreated a node pool at eleven in the morning. The ownership is scoped as narrowly as we could manage — application code, tests, and per-service config under `services/*/config/` are not owned by SRE, so the common cases still self-serve. The condition the product leads asked for before agreeing was a two-hour response target on owner reviews during working hours, and the SRE rota carries it. Ownership entries are reviewed quarterly; two stale team handles have been removed since.

`.github/CODEOWNERS` names teams and never individuals: `services/ledger/** @halyard/billing`, `apps/console/** @halyard/console-guild`, `infra/** @halyard/platform`. Owning paths by person had produced a standing queue in front of two senior engineers who happened to have written most of the original code, and their absence turned into a merge freeze for whatever they owned. Team routing spreads the load, survives holidays, and makes review a normal part of a team's work rather than a favour asked of a specific person. The secondary effect was the point: a reviewer who is not the original author has to read the change, which surfaced three interface assumptions in the first month that the original author would have skimmed past. Teams are kept small enough that ownership still means something — five people or fewer — because a team of twenty owning everything is the same as nobody owning anything. Paths with no obvious team fall through to the platform team by a catch-all entry at the bottom of the file, and that catch-all firing is treated as a signal that the ownership map needs a change.

Review routing was narrowed after the catch-all owner in `.github/CODEOWNERS` was removed. Every repository had begun with a single line assigning `*` to the platform group, which meant three people were nominally responsible for reviewing everything and in practice reviewed by rotation and guesswork; median time to first review had drifted past a day and a half. Ownership is now declared per top-level directory, with `infra/` split further because the Terraform modules and the cluster manifests have different reviewers. Rules that assign more than three people were disallowed — a large owner list reads as an invitation for everyone to assume someone else has it. The file is checked in CI against the group membership API, so an entry naming a disbanded team fails the build rather than silently matching nobody. Median time to first review came back under four hours within a month, and the more useful effect was that reviewers stopped being shown pull requests they had no context for. Unowned paths fail the build too, which forced a short and slightly uncomfortable exercise in deciding who owns the scripts nobody wrote on purpose.

Publishing the component gallery from CI was made opt-in per pull request instead of running on every push. It had been building and deploying a static site on each commit to every branch, roughly two minutes of runner time and a deploy slot spent mostly on branches nobody opened. The demand was concentrated in the few pull requests that changed visual components, and those authors were perfectly willing to ask. Adding a label now triggers the job and the bot comments the preview link; removing the label tears the environment down again. Making it opt-in also trimmed the check list on ordinary backend pull requests, where a gallery deploy failing for an unrelated infrastructure reason was blocking merges and being overridden as a matter of routine. Habitually overriding a required check is worse than not having the check, because it teaches everyone that red is negotiable, so the standing rule is that anything on the required set has to be something we would genuinely stop for.

The warehouse account used by the BI tool now has a hard cap on concurrent sessions, set after a dashboard rebuild starved the nightly load. The warehouse allocates query slots rather than connections, and the BI tool opens one session per tile on a refresh; a single popular dashboard with eighteen tiles could occupy most of the available concurrency for as long as its slowest tile ran. Scheduled extracts, which are the thing the business actually depends on in the morning, were queued behind interactive traffic nobody was watching. The cap is enforced on the service account rather than per user, since the tool multiplexes everything through one identity, and scheduled extracts were moved to a separate account with its own smaller reservation so the two classes of work cannot starve each other. Interactive queries now fail fast when the cap is reached and the tool retries with backoff, which users experience as a slow dashboard rather than a stuck one. This is deliberately not the posture we take on the transactional side, where waiting is cheap and queueing is preferred: warehouse queries are long, so making callers wait converts one slow dashboard into a stalled pipeline.

Docker layer caching for `apps/console` was moved off the runner and off the Actions cache backend onto the container registry, using `--cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/halyard/console:buildcache,mode=max` with the matching `--cache-from`. The runner-local layer store stopped being useful the moment the pool became ephemeral: every job got a fresh instance, so the local cache was always empty and the flag was decorative. The Actions cache backend did work, but the console image plus three service images pushed the repository past its ten-gigabyte quota, and eviction there is least-recently-used across the whole repo, so the frontend cache was routinely evicted by whichever service built most often that week. Registry-backed cache is paid for as storage instead of fought over as a quota, `mode=max` retains intermediate layers so an application-source change still reuses the dependency install layer, and cleanup is a scheduled garbage-collection job we control rather than an eviction race we lose. The measured trade is roughly two dollars a month of storage against about ninety seconds saved on every image build.

`pnpm -F console typecheck` runs as its own job rather than as a step in front of the bundle. The bundler strips types without checking them, so a green build said nothing about type correctness: a pull request that broke a shared interface bundled cleanly and blew up at runtime in review twice before we split them. As separate jobs they run in parallel, so total wall clock is unchanged, and the failing check has the right name, which stopped people reading a build failure and hunting for a bundler problem that was not there. `tsc --noEmit` runs across the whole workspace with incremental mode disabled in CI, because the buildinfo file is one more piece of state to key and invalidate for a check that finishes in under a minute anyway. Lint was folded onto the same runner as typecheck, since both need only the dependency install and neither writes to the output directory.

Container builds moved off the hosted CI runners onto a self-hosted pool of four builders in our own account. The trigger was cost — image builds were the largest single line in the CI bill — but the reason it stuck is cache locality.

Hosted runners start empty. Every build pulled every layer and re-ran the dependency install, so a one-line change to a Python service took eleven minutes end to end. The self-hosted pool keeps a persistent BuildKit cache on local NVMe; the same build now takes two and a half minutes warm and about six cold. Jobs opt in with `runs-on: [self-hosted, builder]` in the workflow file.

The trade we accepted is that the builders are ours to patch and ours to fix when they fill up. A weekly `docker buildx prune --filter until=168h` keeps the cache bounded — before we added it, a builder fell over with a full disk roughly monthly and everyone blamed CI in general.

Test jobs deliberately stayed on hosted runners. They are short, highly parallel, and benefit far more from clean isolation than from a warm cache.

CI publishes every service image with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64` under a single tag. Laptops are arm64 and production nodes are amd64, and before this the local stack ran emulated amd64 images, which were slow enough that people quietly stopped running the stack at all — the behaviour we were trying to encourage was being taxed into extinction. Building natively for both fixed the speed problem and surfaced a real divergence in the process: one Python dependency had no arm64 wheel and fell back to compiling from source, producing a subtly different numeric result in a rate calculation. Building both architectures in CI means that divergence fails a check instead of appearing as a rounding discrepancy in someone's local testing. Base images are pinned by digest rather than tag, so a base image rebuild upstream cannot silently change what either architecture is built on.

Every periodic job is declared in `ops/schedules.yaml` and nowhere else — no decorators scattered through service code, no entries in the platform's own scheduler UI. Each entry carries a `jitter_seconds` value and the manifest linter rejects an entry without one. The reason is a nightly pattern we watched for months: almost everything had been written to run at the top of the hour, so at :00 the fleet opened several hundred database connections simultaneously, the connection pool queued, and unrelated interactive requests timed out for about fifteen seconds every hour. Jitter spread the same work across a window and the spike disappeared without any capacity change. The single manifest solved a different problem, which is that nobody could answer "what runs at 3am" without grepping four repositories, and two jobs had been silently doing overlapping work for a year. The manifest is also what the on-call runbook links to during an incident when the question is whether a scheduled job is implicated. Ad-hoc scheduling is still possible for one-off operational work, but anything that survives past a week is expected to move into the manifest, and the weekly review catches the ones that do not.

Errors raised through the shared outbound HTTP wrapper are given an explicit fingerprint rather than relying on default grouping. The wrapper raises its own exception type from a single line, so the tracker's stack-trace-based grouping collapsed every upstream failure in the company into one issue — carrier timeouts, address-validation outages and our own misconfigured base URLs all landed in the same bucket, which grew past four hundred thousand events and hid three separate incidents inside a graph that always looked busy. The fix sets `fingerprint = ["http-client", upstream_host, str(status_class)]` in the wrapper's capture path, so a carrier's API going down produces its own issue with its own first-seen timestamp and its own alert. Deliberately excluded from the fingerprint: the full URL, because path parameters would shatter one outage into thousands of issues; and the exact status code, because a service flapping between 502 and 504 is one problem, not two. We reviewed the other candidates for custom fingerprints and found none worth the maintenance — default grouping is right almost everywhere, and this wrapper was pathological specifically because it is a single chokepoint that every service's outbound traffic passes through.

Database credentials are leased, not owned. Each role — `invoicing_rw`, `ledger_ro`, and the rest — is configured with `default_ttl = 1h` and `max_ttl = 24h`, and the vault drops the underlying Postgres user when the lease expires. The point is blast radius: a credential lifted from a core dump or a stray log line is worthless within the hour, and we no longer run the quarterly ritual of rotating a shared password across eleven services and discovering the two that were missed by watching them fail. The one-hour figure was tuned rather than chosen. At fifteen minutes the renewal traffic was heavy enough to show up in vault latency percentiles; at eight hours a leaked credential outlived most of our detection paths, which was the whole thing we were buying. Long-running batch work was the awkward case — the nightly reconciliation holds a lease it renews rather than re-issuing, because re-issuing mid-transaction left us with connections owned by two different users and a permissions error at commit time. Revocation doubles as break-glass: cutting off a suspect service is `vault lease revoke -prefix` against its role, and we have rehearsed it twice, once for real when a contractor's laptop went missing.

Failed jobs land in a per-queue dead-letter queue and are re-enqueued only through `ops/bin/replay-dlq`, never by hand. The tool takes a queue and a time window — `replay-dlq --queue jobs.standard --since 2h` — re-stamps each message with a fresh trace identifier that links back to the original attempt, and paces the replay so a thousand recovered jobs do not arrive as one spike at the dependency that just came back. Before it existed, replays were done by an engineer with a Redis client and a for-loop, which produced duplicates twice and, once, replayed a window that included jobs which had already succeeded on a later attempt. The tool refuses to replay a message whose idempotency key has already been observed as completed, which is the guard that makes it safe to run twice when you are not sure whether the first run finished. It also writes an audit line per replay batch with the operator and the window, because after an incident the question "did someone replay this, and when" was consistently hard to answer. Dead letters older than seven days expire; anything worth keeping past a week is a bug report, not a queued job.

Debug-level logging in production is sampled rather than switched off. The shipper applies `log_sample_rate = 0.01` to debug lines and passes info and above through untouched. Sampling is keyed on the request id, so a sampled request is complete — you get every debug line for that request or none of them, never a fragment, which is what makes the sampled lines worth keeping at all.

We arrived here after two failed positions. Debug fully off meant reproducing a production problem required a deploy to turn it on, which took twenty minutes and usually changed the conditions we were trying to observe. Debug fully on meant `checkout-api` alone produced more volume than every other service combined, and the ingest pipeline began shedding during traffic peaks — that is, we lost logs at exactly the moment we needed them.

One percent of complete traces turned out to be plenty. For any problem affecting more than a handful of requests an hour, a sampled example already exists. For the genuinely rare ones, a per-account override raises the rate for a single customer without touching global volume.

The update bot is configured in `renovate.json` with `schedule = ["before 06:00 on monday"]` and a single grouped PR for all non-major bumps, instead of the default one-PR-per-package. At the old cadence the bot opened between nine and twenty PRs a week across the monorepo; each one burned a full matrix run, and the review queue got so noisy that people started merging them unread, which is strictly worse than not bumping at all. Majors are still separated out — `separateMajorMinor` stays true — because those need a human to read a changelog. Security advisories bypass the schedule entirely via `vulnerabilityAlerts`, which opens immediately at any hour and pings the security channel. The tradeoff we accepted is a window of up to seven days where a routine patch release sits unapplied. That was acceptable because our exposure model treats routine patches as low urgency and advisories as the real signal, and advisories are not batched. The grouped PR is expected to be merged or explicitly closed within the same week; a stale bot PR older than fourteen days is treated as a process failure and raised in the platform sync, not silently rebased forever.

Dependency updates arrive as one batched pull request per repository on Monday morning, not as a stream of individual ones. The previous configuration opened a pull request per dependency and produced around thirty a week across the estate; reviewers approved them without reading, which is worse than not reviewing at all because it launders an unexamined change through a process that looks like scrutiny. Batching makes the weekly upgrade a single deliberate task with one person assigned, and a failing test in the batch gets investigated rather than ignored, because there is only one thing to investigate. Security advisories are exempt and still open immediately and individually, since those need to move faster than the weekly cadence. Major version bumps are also excluded from the batch and opened separately with the changelog quoted in the description, because they usually need code changes and burying one among a dozen patch bumps guarantees it gets rubber-stamped. The bot does not auto-merge anything. Upgrade lag is tracked as a number rather than assumed: the oldest outstanding minor version across services sits on the platform dashboard.

Test and tooling packages live in the `dev` dependency group of each service's `pyproject.toml`, and any engineer may add one in the same PR as the work that needs it — no ticket, no platform sign-off. The reasoning was that dev-group packages never reach a container image: the Dockerfile runs `uv sync --no-dev`, so a bad linter plugin can waste CI minutes but cannot page anyone at 3am. We accepted that this lets the group sprawl; it holds around forty entries across the monorepo and nobody has audited it since the uv migration. Two guards keep the sprawl cheap. First, the dev group resolves into the same `uv.lock` as everything else, so a dev package that drags in an incompatible pin of a shared library fails resolution loudly instead of diverging quietly. Second, CI fails if an import of a dev-group package appears under `services/*/src/`; the check is an AST scan in `tools/check_dev_imports.py`, added after a debugging helper shipped inside a request handler and put 80ms of import time on every cold start. The rule engineers actually remember is shorter than the policy text: if it only runs in CI or on a laptop, add it and move on.

`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` is the supported way to get a working toolchain, pinning the Go, Node and Python versions along with the protobuf compiler and the database client. Onboarding used to be a full day of chasing version mismatches, and the failures were the demoralising kind — a build error whose cause is a minor version difference in a code generator nobody thought to mention. With the container, a new engineer runs the test suite within the hour. `scripts/bootstrap.sh` was kept for people who want the toolchain on the host, and it is exercised weekly by a scheduled CI job on a clean image, because roughly half the team refuses the container and an untested escape hatch is a broken escape hatch discovered at the worst moment. The container is not required for anything; it is the path we promise to keep working. The bootstrap script installs the same pinned versions from the same manifest, so the two cannot drift apart silently.

Every service has a daily log volume budget with an alert when it exceeds it. Budgets were derived from the previous quarter's actuals plus 50%, live alongside the service catalogue entry, and the alert (`log_budget_exceeded`) opens a ticket rather than paging.

The problem this solves is that log volume is a shared resource with no natural back-pressure. One team adds a debug line inside a hot loop, ingest cost rises 30% overnight, and nobody notices for a month because the bill arrives quarterly and belongs to nobody in particular. Two of these happened in one year. Both were a single line of code, and both were found by accident.

Budgets are advisory, not enforced. We considered hard per-service rate limiting and decided against it, because the failure mode is dropping logs during exactly the incident that produced the spike — an outage is legitimately the noisiest moment a service will ever have. A ticket the next morning reaches the same outcome without that risk.

Reviewing the budgets is part of the quarterly platform review. Roughly half get raised, which is fine. The point was never the number; the point was noticing.

Private keys for the public edge certificates never enter our vault. Certificates are issued and renewed by the CDN provider, generated inside their hardware modules and not exportable, and the origin certificate is a separate long-lived pair that we do control. We debated bringing everything under one roof for a single audit trail and decided against it. To hold the edge keys ourselves we would first have to be able to export them, which is strictly worse than not being able to, and we would then own the renewal automation, which is the part that most reliably breaks at three in the morning. What we gave up is real: we cannot answer who read that key, only who could have changed the certificate configuration, and the auditors recorded it as an observation rather than a finding. The compensating control is that configuration changes on the edge alert into the security channel and are reviewed weekly against the change log.

Encrypting secrets into the repository was proposed and rejected. The pitch was reasonable: values sit next to the code that uses them, a change is a reviewable diff, and there is no extra service to keep alive during an outage. Two objections killed it. Git history is permanent, so a value that leaks once has leaked in every clone forever, and rotating it becomes rotating it while accepting that the old ciphertext is still out there against the day the encryption is broken. And it moves the key distribution problem rather than solving it — someone still decides which laptops and which build agents hold decryption keys, which is the same access-control question with worse tooling and no revocation story. We also did not want a per-environment value change to require a code review and a deploy; the finance team's gateway credentials should not need a pull request. The decision was written down with the caveat that non-sensitive configuration belongs in the repo and should stay there.

Alerting from the error tracker routes to the owning team's channel, derived from the repository `CODEOWNERS` file. The mapping is generated into `ops/alerting/routes.yaml` by a CI step, so adding a team to CODEOWNERS is the only action needed to start receiving your own alerts. The single shared channel it replaced had the predictable fate: it carried every new issue from every service, people muted it within a month, and a payments regression sat unread for two days in a channel that eleven engineers were nominally watching. Routing by ownership made the volume per channel small enough to read. Two rules keep it working. An issue in a path with no owner routes to the platform channel and is treated as an ownership gap to be fixed, not a permanent destination — that channel is meant to stay near-empty. And the routing key is the file path of the top in-app frame, not the service name, because our shared libraries raise from code owned by a different team than the service that happens to be running. That distinction was the whole reason the naive service-name routing was abandoned.

The tracker SDK is initialized with `traces_sample_rate = 0.02` and `profiles_sample_rate = 0.0`, while error events are captured at full rate. The asymmetry is deliberate and cost-driven. Traces are emitted per request, so at our volume even a few percent produces a usable latency distribution, and the marginal value of the ninety-eighth percent of traces is close to zero — you cannot look at them. Errors are the opposite: they are rare relative to traffic, each one is individually actionable, and a sampled error is a bug someone silently does not fix. Sampling errors also destroys the count, which is the number people actually use to decide whether something is getting worse. One consequence we accepted is that a traced request and an errored request are usually not the same request, so "open the trace for this error" works only two percent of the time. We compensated by making the structured log line carry enough context to reconstruct the request shape without a trace. The sample rate is set in `libs/observability/init.py` and is intentionally not per-service configurable; every attempt to let teams tune it locally ended with someone setting it to 1.0 during an investigation and leaving it there.

Each integration run gets its own throwaway Postgres. `docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml up -d db` starts it with the data directory on tmpfs and `-c fsync=off -c full_page_writes=off`, which is reckless for a real database and correct for one that lives eleven minutes. Schema comes from the same migration files production uses, applied once into a template database that each case clones with `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE`, so a case starts from a known state in about ninety milliseconds instead of replaying two hundred and forty migrations. We used to point the suite at a long-lived local database that developers reused across runs, and the failures it produced were unreproducible: a case passed on a laptop that happened to hold a row left over from a manual poke three weeks earlier, and failed on a fresh checkout. Throwing the container away afterwards is the whole point. The template-clone trick saved roughly nine minutes on a full run and is the reason we could afford a real database at all instead of mocking the data layer and testing our mocks.

Structured JSON logging is mandatory and the shipper silently drops anything that does not parse as an object. Four fields are required on every line: `request_id`, `service`, `level`, and `ts`. Everything else is free-form.

`request_id` is generated at the edge, propagated through every internal call in a header, and is the single reason cross-service debugging is tractable. Before it existed, following one customer request through checkout, the ledger, and the notification relay meant grepping three streams by timestamp and hoping. Now it is one query with one filter.

Enforcement is deliberately blunt. We tried a linter, then a log-format warning, then a dashboard naming non-compliant services, and none of them moved the number meaningfully. Dropping unparseable lines moved it to zero in nine days, because the first time a team could not find their own logs during an incident, they fixed their logger that afternoon.

Free-form message text is still allowed and still useful, but nothing queries it. Anything a dashboard or an alert depends on has to be its own field, which also broke the habit of formatting numbers into English sentences and then regexing them back out.

Experiment assignment does not run through the flag service. A/B tests live in the analytics platform, which owns assignment, exposure logging, and the statistics, and the two systems are deliberately not connected.

They look similar enough that the proposal to merge them resurfaces regularly. The difference that matters is what each is for. A release flag is an operational control: engineers flip it, it is expected to reach a terminal state, and the only question it answers is whether the new code path is live. An experiment is a measurement instrument: it needs a pre-registered hypothesis, a fixed sample size, exposure events tied to a specific user action, and someone's opinion about when it is legitimate to stop looking. Running experiments through an operational control invites people to peek at partial results and stop early, which is how you manufacture confident nonsense.

There is a genuine cost to the split. A feature that is both gradually rolled out and measured needs two mechanisms, and the two can disagree about who is in which arm. Engineers occasionally build an experiment out of a release flag simply because it is nearer to hand. We accept that and correct it in review, rather than merging the systems and losing the distinction entirely.

Finance queries a dedicated read replica, never the billing primary. The replica is `billing_ro`, analyst accounts hold `SELECT` on the reporting views only and not on base tables, and replica lag above ninety seconds alerts the data team. This exists because a month-end query against the primary once held locks long enough that the payment retry worker backed up and about four hundred charges were attempted hours late. The views layer matters as much as the replica does. Analysts asked for direct table access and we pushed back, because three columns in the base schema mean different things depending on a status field, and every ad-hoc query ever written against them has been wrong in the same way. The views encode that logic once, in one place, reviewed by someone who knows it. The cost is that a genuinely new question sometimes needs a view change and a day of turnaround, which finance accepted in exchange for numbers that reconcile. Nothing writes to the replica, and each team gets a distinct user so we can see whose query is running.

Anyone in their first eight weeks on the codebase gets a second reviewer on every pull request, regardless of seniority or employment type. This was originally drafted as a rule about contractors and was rewritten, because the thing being addressed is a context gap rather than a trust question, and a principal engineer who joined last Tuesday has exactly the same gap. The specific failures it catches are the ones no amount of care prevents without local knowledge: touching a table that has a downstream consumer nobody documented, logging a field that falls under the data-handling policy, or reimplementing a helper that already exists two directories over. The second reviewer is expected to be someone with long tenure, and their job is context rather than correctness. The window is time-based rather than count-based on purpose, so nobody games it by opening trivial pull requests, and it lapses automatically without anyone having to declare a person ready.

Every flag change emits a `flag_changed` event carrying the key, the old and new state, the actor, and the environment, and those events land in the same channel and the same annotation stream as deploys.

The reason is incident correlation. Roughly a third of our incidents are caused by an intentional change, and for a long time the first question — what changed in the last hour — could only be answered for deploys. Flag flips were invisible unless someone thought to open the flag console and read its audit tab, which nobody does in the first ten minutes of an incident. Putting both on one timeline turned that question into a single glance at an annotation overlay.

It changed behaviour more than we expected. Making flips visible to everyone rather than private to the person flipping introduced a mild social check, and people started writing a sentence about why in the change note, unprompted, because they knew someone would read it.

Those events also feed the rollout dashboards, drawing the percentage-over-time line for a flag. That panel turned out to be the most-used thing we have during a gradual rollout.

Creating a flag requires more than a name. The registry rejects anything without an owning team, a link to the ticket that motivated it, and a one-line description of what being enabled means. Names are `snake_case` and prefixed by domain — `checkout_`, `ledger_`, `growth_` — which is the only reason the flag list is readable at a glance rather than an undifferentiated wall of three hundred entries.

The description field is the one that earns its keep. We required it after repeatedly finding flags whose names were ambiguous about polarity: `disable_new_pricing` being off means new pricing is on, and reading that at 02:00 during an incident goes wrong about half the time. The description has to state what happens when the flag is enabled, in one sentence, and reviewers are told to actually read it rather than approve past it.

Owner is a team, never an individual. We started with individuals and learned the obvious lesson when two of them left, leaving behind flags nobody would claim and nobody dared touch.

None of this is enforced at the call site — a key can be read before it is registered — but an unregistered key appearing in evaluation telemetry opens a ticket against the calling service.

In tests, every flag evaluates to its registered default and the flag client never touches the network. Overriding is explicit: a `with_flag("checkout_new_pricing", True)` context manager in the Python services and an equivalent fixture in the Go ones.

The rule we enforce in review is that a test exercising flagged behaviour must exist in both states. Not because both are equally interesting, but because the failure we kept hitting was a feature shipped behind a flag, tested only in the enabled state, and quietly broken in the disabled one — which is the state production is actually in until a rollout finishes, and the state a rollback returns to. Two incidents came from exactly that shape: the flag went to 100%, someone found a problem, the flag went back to 0%, and the old path had rotted because nothing had exercised it in six weeks.

Reading a flag straight from the global client inside a unit test is a review failure. It works, but it couples the test to whatever the registry happens to say today, and we once had a suite start failing because someone changed a default in a different repository.

Flag evaluation is in-process against a snapshot, never a network call. Each pod polls the flag service every thirty seconds (`flag_poll_interval = 30s`), receives the entire ruleset as one document, and evaluates locally. A pod that cannot reach the service keeps serving from the last snapshot it holds and logs a staleness warning; it never blocks and never fails closed.

We rebuilt it this way because the first version made an RPC per evaluation, and `checkout-api` evaluates eleven flags on the hot path. That added measurable latency and, far worse, made the flag service a hard dependency of the payment path — a component everyone had been treating as a convenience suddenly carried the availability requirements of the ledger.
