The cost of the snapshot model is propagation delay. A flip takes up to thirty seconds to be true everywhere, and during that window different pods disagree. Every consumer therefore has to tolerate two requests from the same user getting different answers, which mostly means not using a flag to decide something that must stay stable within a session.

A snapshot is also baked into the image as a fallback, so a cold start with the flag service down still has sane defaults.

A test that fails intermittently gets `@pytest.mark.quarantine` and a dated entry in `docs/flaky-register.md`, and the default invocation is `pytest -m "not quarantine"`. Quarantine expires after two weeks: either the owner has fixed it or the test is deleted. We arrived here after a stretch where the suite carried eleven known-flaky cases, everyone re-ran CI on red by reflex, and a genuine regression sat undetected for three days because it looked like the usual noise. The delete-on-expiry rule was contentious — removing a test feels like removing coverage — but a test nobody trusts already provides no coverage, and making deletion automatic turned an ignorable nag into a deadline. Quarantined cases still run in the nightly job and their pass rate is reported, which is often what identifies the cause; the ones that failed only after midnight UTC were all timezone-boundary bugs in the test rather than the code. Since the policy landed the register has never held more than three entries at once.

The console application and the design system stay in a single repository, `kestrel-web`, with the library at `packages/ui` and consumers under `apps/`. This was a deliberate exception, argued and granted rather than inherited. A token change — a spacing scale, a semantic colour — touches the library and every consumer of it, and keeping them together means one pull request carries the change, the call-site updates and the visual regression snapshots, reviewed as a unit. Split apart, the same change becomes publish, wait, bump, fix, with a window in the middle where the two are inconsistent. The design system is also published to the internal registry on tag for the two services outside this repository that render server-side email templates; those consumers accept the lag. The boundary is enforced rather than assumed: `packages/ui` may not import from `apps/`, checked by a lint rule in CI, so the shared code stays genuinely shared and the repository does not quietly become one application with a library-shaped folder in it. Ownership is declared per directory. If the design system ever gains a consumer with a different release cadence than the console, this decision should be reopened.

The limiter uses a GCRA cell-rate algorithm implemented as a Lua script in `ops/redis/gcra.lua`, replacing the fixed-window counter it started with. Fixed windows let a client spend a full allowance in the last second of one window and another full allowance in the first second of the next, which in practice meant a burst of double the nominal rate arriving at a service that had been provisioned for the nominal rate. We saw it as a recurring pattern of latency spikes at minute boundaries that took two on-call shifts to attribute. GCRA smooths this by tracking a theoretical arrival time per key rather than a count per bucket, so a client that spends its burst has to wait proportionally before the next request is admitted. It is also a single round trip — one `EVALSHA` returning both the decision and the remaining allowance — which matters because the limiter runs on every request. Sliding-window-log was rejected: it is more accurate still, but it stores a timestamp per request and our highest-volume keys would have made the memory footprint per client unbounded during exactly the traffic surges we care most about surviving.

During a declared incident, a change may merge without a prior approving review. Waiting for a reviewer at three in the morning costs more than the risk carried by a one-line change, and in practice the wait was producing worse outcomes than the change ever did — people either sat on a known fix or quietly used admin override, which is the same exception without the paper trail. The exception is narrow. The incident commander has to acknowledge it in the channel, the change must be a revert, a feature-flag flip, or a configuration value, and anything larger goes through the normal path however inconvenient that is. A real review is filed within one business day, tracked as a follow-up on the incident, and the incident is not closed until it lands. Recording the exception in the timeline matters more than the rule itself: it means we can look back at a quarter and see how often the escape hatch was used, and whether it was ever used outside an actual incident.

Removal is owner-driven and staged, not opportunistic. Anyone can notice that a package looks unused, but only the owning service team may delete it, and the deletion happens in two steps across two releases. First the package is marked deprecated in the service's dependency notes and any remaining imports are removed; the release ships with the package still installed. Only after that release has been in production for a full week does a second PR drop it from the manifest. The two-step exists because dynamic imports and plugin-style entry points do not show up in a static import scan, and we lost an evening to exactly that when a serialization backend was removed and only failed on a code path that ran once a day. The static scan is still the starting point — it produces the candidate list — but a clean scan is treated as evidence, not proof. Unowned packages, the ones that predate the current team boundaries, are the hard case. Those are not removed unilaterally; they go on the platform backlog and get an owner assigned before anything is touched. We would rather carry a few kilobytes of dead weight for a quarter than discover ownership through an outage.

Pool sizing for `dispatch-worker` was settled by measurement rather than by copying the numbers from `booking-api`. The worker runs 24 replicas with 8 concurrent consumers each, and the inherited configuration asked the pooler for 192 server connections against a primary that tops out near 400 backends, leaving nothing for `ledger` or `rates-engine`. Two rounds of load testing showed throughput flat between 6 and 20 server connections per pool: the worker's transactions are short, median 4ms and p99 38ms, so the bottleneck is queue depth, not connections. We set `default_pool_size = 6` on the dispatch database entry and raised `max_client_conn = 900` so bursts wait in the pooler instead of failing at connect time. The rule written down afterwards: size a pool to the service's concurrent in-flight transaction count under normal load, never to replica count times worker concurrency, and let clients queue where the wait is cheap and observable. The single trigger for revisiting is sustained client waiting in `SHOW POOLS` — anything above zero for more than a minute means the pool is genuinely undersized rather than merely busy. Two services have since been sized the same way and neither needed more than eight.

Pooler metrics come from a sidecar exporter that connects to the admin console and runs `SHOW POOLS` and `SHOW STATS` every fifteen seconds, translating the rows into Prometheus gauges. The exporter authenticates as a stats-only role that cannot issue `RELOAD` or `KILL`; an exporter with operational privileges is an outage waiting for a bad config push. Client waiting count per pool is the series that alerts. Application-side metrics were assumed sufficient at first and were not — a client blocked on acquiring a connection looks identical to a client waiting on a slow server, and only the pooler can distinguish them. The scrape interval was kept deliberately short relative to the alert window, since waiting counts are instantaneous values and a sixty-second scrape missed several real stalls during testing. Dashboards are per pool rather than aggregated, because the aggregate hid one saturated database entry sitting next to three idle ones.

Each integration test run creates its own database with `createdb -T halyard_test_template`, exports it as `PGDATABASE` for the worker, and drops it at the end. Previously all runs shared one test database, and two CI runs overlapping meant one truncating tables out from under the other. It presented as impossible flakes — assertions failing on rows the test had definitely just inserted — and cost about a week of collective confusion before anyone suspected the environment rather than the code. Using a template database rather than running migrations per run keeps creation at roughly two hundred milliseconds, so the isolation is essentially free; the template itself is rebuilt whenever the migration set changes, keyed on a hash of the revision directory. A janitor job drops test databases older than a day, because runs killed mid-flight never reach their cleanup and the leftovers otherwise accumulate until the instance hits its connection or storage limits.

Integration tests never run against shared staging. This was settled the afternoon a suite truncated the customer table in staging during a sales demo, but the argument stands on its own: a shared environment holds other people's state, so a test either tolerates unknown data, in which case its assertions are weak, or it controls the environment, in which case it is hostile to everyone else using it. Each run now brings up its own dependencies and tears them down afterwards. What we gave up is the thing shared staging was genuinely good at — catching configuration and networking problems that only appear in a real deployment — so that coverage moved into a small set of post-deploy smoke checks that run against staging after every promotion and are permitted to touch nothing but read paths and one dedicated test account. Staging is now a place humans look at rather than a place tests fight over, and the demo team stopped asking us to freeze deploys before customer calls.

Service-to-service calls inside the mesh are not rate limited. The gateway distinguishes them by the mTLS peer identity — anything presenting a workload certificate under `spiffe://halyard.io/ns/prod/` skips the limiter filter entirely — and never by a header, because a header can be forged by an external client and a certificate cannot. The reasoning is that rate limiting is the wrong tool for internal traffic. Internal callers are not adversarial and not unknown; when one of them overwhelms a dependency, the answer is backpressure and concurrency limits at the callee, which shed load in a way that preserves the caller's ability to retry sensibly. A 429 to an internal caller just converts a capacity problem into a retry storm. The one nuance is the internal proxy that fronts partner integrations: it holds a workload certificate but forwards traffic that ultimately originated outside, so it is explicitly excluded from the bypass and its forwarded requests are limited against the originating partner's key. That exclusion is asserted in a test in `tests/gateway/test_identity_bypass.py`, because it is the kind of thing that would silently regress the next time the mesh config is refactored.

The shared developer CLI is published to the internal package registry and pinned by each consumer, rather than copied into repositories as it used to be. Vendoring started as a convenience and became a liability: four repositories carried four versions of the same script, three of them subtly different, and a fix to the deploy helper had to be applied by hand in each place, which meant it was usually applied in two. Nobody could tell which version was running from reading a build log. Publishing makes the version an explicit fact in each repository's lockfile, so a bug report is answered by asking which version rather than by diffing four copies of a file. It also made deprecation possible, since a command can warn for a release before it disappears. The cost is that a change now takes a release rather than an edit, so the tool grew a way to run from a local checkout during development.

Invoice and ledger data carries a seven-year retention obligation, and that obligation is served by a separate pipeline rather than by extending the backups' retention. A monthly export writes the closed period to a bucket with object lock in compliance mode and `retain_until` set seven years out, which means nobody — including the account root — can delete or overwrite those objects before the date. Operational backups keep their own much shorter window and are free to age out, which is the point of the split: folding a legal requirement into the backup lifecycle makes the backup policy impossible to tune without a lawyer in the room. The export is a stable documented format rather than a database dump, because a seven-year-old dump assumes a database version that will not exist and reading it becomes a project. Legal hold is a separate flag applied at the prefix level and is documented in the ops runbook alongside the named role permitted to apply it. The retention dates themselves are reviewed once a year against the obligation, since the obligation is the thing that changes.

Job signatures accept primitives and identifiers only — `def rebuild_manifest(shipment_id: str, *, force: bool = False)` is the shape — and the broker is configured with `task_serializer = "json"` so passing anything richer fails at enqueue time rather than at execution. The rule came from a deploy that changed a model's field set while several hundred pickled instances were sitting in the queue; the old objects deserialized into the new class and workers crashed in ways that took most of an afternoon to understand, because the traceback pointed at the consumer and the cause was the producer from twenty minutes earlier. Passing an identifier means the job re-reads current state, which is almost always what you actually wanted: a job that runs four minutes after enqueue should act on the row as it is now, not as it was. The visible cost is an extra database read per job, which we measured and found irrelevant next to the work the jobs do. The one place this bites is jobs that genuinely need the prior value — a few audit paths — and those pass the specific scalar they need explicitly, which also makes the dependency legible in the signature instead of hidden inside a serialized blob.

`tariff-svc` was granted a standing exception and still opens its own connections directly to the primary. Two things in it are incompatible with transaction-level pooling: it uses LISTEN/NOTIFY to invalidate its rate-band cache when a pricing rule changes, and its nightly recalculation builds session-scoped temporary tables that it queries across several statements. Both depend on a stable session, which a transaction pooler does not provide, and running that one database entry in session mode would have pinned server connections for the life of every client connection and given up most of the benefit anyway. The exception carries conditions. The service's own pool is capped at 20 connections, enforced in `tariff_svc/db.py` and asserted in a startup check so a config typo cannot quietly triple it. Its role has a connection limit set at the database level as a second line of defence. The recalculation job is the only writer allowed to hold a session longer than a minute, and it runs against the standby where possible. The rewrite that would remove the dependency — moving invalidation onto the existing message bus and replacing temp tables with a materialised staging table — is scoped but has never been urgent enough to schedule. Until it lands, treat `tariff-svc` connection counts as fixed overhead when sizing anything else on that primary.

Kill switches are treated as a distinct class of flag with different change control. A kill switch is one whose only job is to turn a dependency or a feature off in an emergency — the fraud-scoring bypass, the notification suspend, read-only mode on the ledger — and flipping one in production requires a second person's approval in the console before it takes effect.

The two-person rule exists because these are the flags whose accidental flip is itself an outage. An ordinary release flag fails toward a slightly different experience; a kill switch flipped by mistake stops something important from happening at all. We had one flipped by a mistyped search in the console, which is a class of accident that no amount of care prevents and a confirmation step does.

The obvious objection is that approval slows down exactly the moment where speed matters most. We measured it during a game day and it added about ninety seconds, comfortably inside the window in which a human is still deciding what to do. During a declared incident the requirement can be waived by the incident commander, and the waiver is recorded.

Kill switches are also exercised quarterly. An emergency control that has never been tested is not a control.

Engineers can read staging secrets from their laptops, read-only, through a short-lived token. `alx login` exchanges the SSO session for an eight-hour vault token scoped to the `staging/` prefix, and `alx secrets read staging/invoicing --field=api_base` prints one field to stdout rather than dumping a whole map — a deliberate choice to discourage people from piping the lot into a local dotfile and forgetting it exists. Production has no equivalent path. Reading a production value requires a break-glass request with a second approver and notifies the security channel, and in practice the answer to "I need the production value to debug this" has been to reproduce it in staging. This closed out our worst habit, which was credentials pasted into chat threads by someone who was blocked at six in the evening. Staging values share nothing with production and rotate automatically each month, so a staging leak is embarrassing rather than an incident. Every issuance is logged with the requesting identity.

When the limiter's Redis backend is unreachable or times out, GET and HEAD requests are admitted and everything else is rejected with 429. The split came out of an incident where the limiter cluster hit its memory ceiling and began evicting counter keys under an LRU policy. The limiter treated a missing key as a fresh allowance, so every request looked like a first request and the fleet took roughly nine minutes of unlimited traffic before anyone connected the two facts. The postmortem's finding was not "make Redis more reliable" but "decide what the limiter does when it cannot decide." Reads fail open because the downstream services have their own concurrency limits and a read flood degrades latency rather than corrupting anything. Writes fail closed because an unbounded write flood is the case where the limiter is actually load-bearing. Two mechanical changes shipped with it: the counter keyspace moved to its own instance with `maxmemory-policy noeviction`, so pressure surfaces as errors instead of silent misses, and `ratelimit_backend_errors_total` now alerts at any sustained non-zero rate rather than on a threshold, because the only acceptable number of backend errors is approximately zero.

Local development is served over https on `*.localtest.halyard.dev`, a public DNS wildcard that resolves to 127.0.0.1, so nobody edits `/etc/hosts` and every developer gets consistent hostnames. The certificate and its private key live in the shared secrets vault and are fetched by `just certs` into a gitignored directory. Plain http locally was producing a specific and recurring class of bug: secure and SameSite cookie attributes behave differently, service worker registration is restricted to secure contexts, and two embedded third-party widgets refuse to load at all. All of those first appeared in staging, days after the change that caused them, with the local reproduction being "it works on my machine" in the most literal sense. Because this is a genuine certificate for a genuine public name, the key is handled as a secret even though it only ever protects loopback traffic: vault-only distribution, never committed, and rotated annually. A leaked key for a name that resolves to localhost is a small problem, but small is not zero and the handling cost is trivial.

`just up` wraps `docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up -d` and brings up Postgres, Redis and a MinIO bucket standing in for object storage. Application services are not in that file: the service you are working on runs on the host, against those dependencies. The split was deliberate after an attempt to containerise everything. Bind-mounted source on macOS made the edit-reload loop take six to eight seconds where the host process took under one, and a loop that slow changes how people work — they batch changes, stop running things locally, and find out in CI. Dependencies do not need a fast loop, so they stay in containers where version pinning is easy and cleanup is a single command. The Postgres container carries `mem_limit: 2g` because it otherwise grew until laptops started swapping during the test suite. Ports are fixed rather than randomised so that a stale connection string in someone's editor config fails loudly instead of connecting to the wrong thing.

Jobs that routinely run longer than a few minutes were moved onto their own worker deployment with a much longer termination grace period. The shared pool's grace period is short by design so that rolling deploys finish quickly, and the consequence was that every deploy killed whatever long job happened to be mid-flight. Those jobs then retried from the beginning, which meant that during a busy release day a thirty-minute reconciliation run could be started and killed four times without ever completing — and because each attempt looked like a normal retry, the pattern was invisible until someone noticed the job had not produced output in two days. Isolating them let us set a generous grace period without slowing ordinary deploys, and let those workers drain rather than restart on a config change. It also made the failure honest: a long job that gets killed now signals loudly instead of quietly retrying forever. The tradeoff is a second pool to size and pay for, mostly idle. We judged that cheaper than the alternative we considered, which was making every long job resumable from a checkpoint. That would have been better engineering and roughly ten times the work, and only three jobs actually needed it.

Merged branches are deleted sixty days after their pull request closes. `.github/workflows/branch-reaper.yml` runs weekly, lists branches whose tip is an ancestor of the trunk, and issues `git push origin --delete` for anything past the window; unmerged branches are only reported, never touched. We had grown to 2,300 remote branches in the platform repo, which made tab-completion useless and pushed a full clone past a minute on the office connection. The sixty-day delay exists because people do go back to a merged branch to recover a dropped commit or a deleted test, usually within a fortnight, and someone's local reflog is not a plan. Protected patterns — the trunk, `release/*`, and `hotfix/*` — are excluded in the workflow config rather than by naming convention, so a branch that accidentally matches cannot be reaped.

Metrics retention is thirteen months. The number is not arbitrary: it is twelve plus one, so any year-over-year comparison has both endpoints available with a month of slack for whoever is late doing the capacity review.

Storage economics make this affordable in a way they are not for other telemetry. Downsampling collapses raw fifteen-second samples into five-minute aggregates after fourteen days, and into one-hour aggregates after ninety, so the tail of the window costs a small fraction of the head. Configured as `retention_period = 395d` on the long-term store, with the downsampling rules in the same file.

We keep metrics this long because the questions they answer are seasonal. Peak load is a Black Friday number, capacity planning is an annual conversation, and for a long time the honest answer to "is this slower than it was last year" was that we did not know. Per-request telemetry answers questions about things that happened recently, and nobody has ever asked to see an individual request from eleven months ago.

The one restriction: alert rules may not query beyond thirty days. Long-window queries against the downsampled tiers are slow enough to make the alerting engine miss evaluations.

Every revision opens with `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '3s'` and `SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '30s'`. The reason is the lock queue. An ALTER TABLE waiting on ACCESS EXCLUSIVE sits behind whatever long-running read is already holding a share lock, and every query arriving afterwards queues behind the ALTER, including the trivial ones. A maintenance operation that should have taken two seconds took the API down for eleven minutes, and the ALTER itself was never the problem — the queue behind it was. Failing fast and retrying a minute later is strictly better, because a lock timeout aborts one statement instead of stalling the whole table. Concurrent index builds are the deliberate exception: they run outside a transaction with the statement timeout raised, in their own revision, flagged in the pull request title so nobody assumes the usual timing. Those revisions are also the ones checked afterwards for an invalid index left behind by an interrupted build, since that failure is quiet and only shows up as a query plan that stopped using the index.

Timing rehearsal moved off staging and onto a full-size scrubbed restore of production, refreshed weekly. Staging's database was about a tenth of production's size, so the numbers it produced were not merely imprecise, they were misleading in a specific direction: everything looked fast. A table rewrite that finished in four seconds there took nine minutes against the real row count, and that gap was discovered during a deploy rather than before one. Any revision touching a table above the threshold row count must now be run against the full-size copy first, with the wall-clock timing pasted into the pull request. The environment sits inside the same network boundary and access controls as production, because a complete copy of the data is production data by any honest reading even after contact details and payment identifiers are scrubbed on restore. Treating it as a lower tier because of the label on it would have been the kind of convenient reasoning that shows up later in an incident report.

`alembic upgrade head` runs as a dedicated job in `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` before the new task definition is registered, not from the application's startup path. Running it at boot meant every replica raced for the same advisory lock, so N-1 containers sat blocked while one migrated, and a failing migration became a crash loop that paged as an application outage and took twenty minutes to correctly attribute. Separating them makes the failure land on a deploy step with the migration's own log output. The split also let us split grants: the runtime role `pier_app` holds DML only, while `pier_migrator` holds DDL and is used exclusively by that job with credentials the application containers never receive. That was the larger win. An application-level SQL injection against a role that cannot create or drop anything has a much smaller ceiling, and the constraint is enforced by the database rather than by careful coding.

The team agreed that a review comment opening with "nit" is explicitly optional: the author may resolve it without changing anything and no one is entitled to be annoyed. Everything else is treated as blocking. This came out of a pattern where reviewers left preferences about naming and file layout in the same voice as genuine defects, and authors, unable to tell the difference, changed everything and shipped a day later. The complementary half of the agreement is that a blocking comment must say what actually breaks — a failing case, a violated invariant, an operational consequence — and a request for changes must state what would satisfy it. "I would have done this differently" is a nit by definition. Two people preferring different structures is not a defect, and the reviewer who feels strongly is welcome to open their own pull request afterwards. The convention did not stop taste debates but it moved them out of the blocking path, which was the whole objective.

Services do not depend on a shared domain-model package. There was one, briefly, holding the shipment and consignment types, and it was retired after it became the tightest coupling in the system: any change to a field meant a coordinated release of four services, and because nobody wanted coordinated releases, the package accumulated optional fields that meant different things in different consumers. What replaced it is duplication on purpose. Each service defines the shape it actually consumes, validates at the boundary, and ignores fields it does not care about. The contract lives in the published API schema, not in a Python class two services happen to import. Drift is real and we accepted it; the failure mode of drift is a service quietly ignoring a new field, which is recoverable, versus the failure mode of shared types, which was a release train nobody could stop. The narrow exception is genuinely mechanical code with no business meaning — logging setup, the tracing initializer, the retry helpers. Those live in shared libraries because their interfaces do not encode product decisions, so they change on their own schedule without dragging anyone along.

The default requirement dropped from two approving reviews to one. Two approvals everywhere roughly doubled the time a change sat waiting and we could not find any corresponding defect reduction in the incident record — the second approval was overwhelmingly a rubber stamp on an already-approved diff. Two are still required where the blast radius warrants it: anything under `services/ledger/**`, anything under `infra/terraform/**`, and any change to authentication middleware. Because branch protection cannot express a per-path approval count, this is enforced by a required check in `.github/workflows/approvals.yml` that inspects the changed paths and the review list and fails when the count is short. That check is deliberately dumb and readable, because a policy nobody can audit is a policy nobody trusts. The tradeoff was made explicit at the time: we are buying latency back on the ninety percent of changes that are ordinary, and paying it on the ten percent where a mistake moves money or takes production down.

The customs-document consumer was left on the old broker when everything else migrated, and that is a deliberate endpoint, not an unfinished migration. It is a single consumer, it processes a few hundred messages a day, and its producer is a partner system that publishes over a protocol the new broker does not speak without an adapter we would then own forever. Porting it was estimated at several weeks, most of that spent re-certifying the document flow with the customs broker, and the benefit would have been retiring one small always-on instance. The contract that flow serves expires within the year and the replacement integration is already specified against the new broker, so the migration work would have been thrown away almost immediately. What we did instead was write down the conditions under which this decision flips: if the old broker needs a version upgrade, if a second consumer ever needs the same messages, or if the contract renews. Any one of those makes porting the cheaper option. The risk we are carrying is that this consumer has no one who has touched it in months, so its runbook was rewritten and a synthetic message runs through it daily to prove the path still works.

A proposal to split the pager into per-service rotations was declined in the spring, and the reasoning is worth keeping because the proposal returns roughly every other quarter.

The argument for splitting was ownership: the payments team knows the ledger, the growth team knows the web front end, and a generalist often cannot do much more than restart something. All true. What killed it was volume. Across the whole platform we take about three pages a week. Split six ways, most rotations would fire less than once a month — and a rotation that never fires is one where nobody remembers how the tooling works, where runbooks go stale unnoticed, and where the person holding the pager is not actually prepared to answer it. Rarity does not make on-call easier; it makes it worse.

We kept one shared rotation and paid for the ownership gap a different way. Every service has a named owning team in the service catalogue, and the responder's job during a page is explicitly to stabilise rather than to fix. Diagnosis is allowed to wait for the people who wrote the code, and saying "I made it stop and I do not know why" is an acceptable outcome.

There is exactly one shared staging environment and it is owned by whoever holds release duty that week. Staging exists to answer a single question — does the release candidate work against production-shaped configuration and the real third-party sandboxes — and that question requires an environment that is long-lived, stable, and wired to integrations that cannot be faked convincingly. Rotating ownership with release duty means it always has an owner, so a broken staging is somebody's job rather than everybody's background irritation. The rule that made it useful was narrowing what deploys there: staging tracks the release branch and nothing else. Feature branches do not go there. Before that, staging was whatever had been pushed most recently, which meant a red staging carried no information at all — the first question was always whose half-finished work was on it, and the answer was usually that nobody remembered. An environment that cannot produce a trustworthy signal is worse than no environment, because people keep spending time on it anyway.

Out-of-hours pages are compensated with time, not money. Anyone woken between 22:00 and 07:00 takes the following morning off with no approval and no explanation, and if the incident ran past 03:00 they take the whole day. We do not track it, and managers were told explicitly not to ask.

We chose time over a per-shift stipend after watching a stipend model at another company turn on-call into something people competed for, which is precisely the wrong incentive — it rewards the people who benefit from a noisy pager, and so the pager never gets quieter. Paying in rest keeps the incentive pointed at reducing pages, because the only way to stop losing mornings is to fix the thing that woke you.

The rule is deliberately generous and deliberately unaudited. The cost of someone occasionally taking a morning they did not strictly earn is far lower than the cost of a rotation that quietly resents itself, and every mechanism we could think of for policing it would have cost more in goodwill than it recovered in hours.

Webhook delivery is throttled per destination endpoint, with a small fixed concurrency and a circuit breaker that opens after sustained failures. This is a separate mechanism from anything on the inbound path and it protects the customer, not us. The trigger was a bulk status update on a large account that generated tens of thousands of events in a few minutes; we delivered them as fast as our workers could, and the customer's receiving endpoint fell over. They were, reasonably, unhappy that our idea of a successful integration was one that took their service down. Pacing per destination rather than per account was chosen because several accounts share hosted integration endpoints, and the thing with finite capacity is the endpoint. When the breaker opens, events queue rather than drop, and delivery resumes with a gradual ramp instead of releasing the whole backlog at once — the first version released everything on recovery and knocked the same endpoint down a second time. Customers can see their own delivery lag in the dashboard, which turned a support-ticket conversation into a self-service one.

Giving every engineer a full personal environment was proposed and rejected on cost. The application tier is cheap and scales to nothing when idle; the datastores are not, and a full stack per engineer means a database instance, a cache, a broker and a search index sitting mostly idle at a per-head monthly figure that came out higher than the entire staging line item multiplied by the size of the team. The benefit was real — no contention, no cleanup, no coordinating over who is testing what — but the contention it removes amounts to a few minutes a week for most people and is concentrated almost entirely in one team's work. What we adopted instead was ephemeral namespaces for the application tier, created per pull request and destroyed on merge, which eliminates the common case of two people deploying incompatible code at the same time. The decision would change if datastores became cheap to provision per developer; a serverless tier with genuine scale-to-zero would do it, and that possibility is worth rechecking annually rather than assuming the arithmetic is stable.

Overrides that lift a specific API key above its plan's allowance are granted through the account record, not by editing gateway config, and every override must carry three things: the requesting account manager, a written reason, and an expiry date no more than one quarter out. Before this, overrides were applied ad hoc during onboarding pushes and never revisited. By the time anyone counted, roughly a fifth of large accounts held a permanent uplift that nobody had capacity-planned for, which meant the numbers we sized the fleet against were fiction. Expiry forces the conversation to happen again while there is still someone who remembers why. Renewal is deliberately easy — a one-line approval from the same manager — because the goal is visibility, not friction. What is not allowed is an override with no end date; the system refuses to store one. Overrides also do not travel with a plan upgrade: if an account moves to a tier whose allowance already covers the uplift, the override is closed rather than stacked on top, which was a real source of accounts running at several times their nominal entitlement without anyone intending it.

Full-stack preview environments per pull request were costed and turned down. Each preview needed its own database, its own queue namespace and its own set of integration credentials, and the carrier sandboxes we test against issue credentials per account rather than per environment with a shared rate limit. Twenty concurrent previews would have exhausted that quota and broken the sandboxes for everyone, including the release verification that actually matters. The infrastructure spend was significant but secondary; the quota was the hard blocker. Examining what people actually wanted previews for, it was overwhelmingly visual review of frontend changes, and that is satisfied by a static preview of the built console pointed at a mock API. So the frontend gets a preview per pull request and the backend does not get an environment at all. The revisit condition was written down rather than left implicit: if the carrier sandbox ever supports per-environment credentials, the main objection disappears and the cost question can be argued on its own merits.

Deployment moved from a weekly release train to per-service tagging. Under the train, everything shipped Thursday at the same version, which meant a failing smoke test in `notify-worker` held back a `ledger` fix that had been ready since Monday, and a revert reverted everything. Releases are now cut per service with a namespaced tag — `git tag ledger/v1.12.0 && git push origin ledger/v1.12.0` — and the pipeline matches `refs/tags/*/v*`, deriving the component name from the tag prefix and deploying only that one. Rollback is the previous tag for that service. The version number is no longer a global fact about the system, which took some getting used to in incident review; the compensating change was a deployment ledger recording what was running everywhere at any timestamp, since nobody could answer that from the tag list alone. Services with a compatibility relationship declare it in their schema version constraint rather than relying on shipping together, and that is the part that made the whole thing safe. Shipping frequency roughly tripled in the following quarter while changes per deploy fell, which is the effect that actually reduced incidents.

Redaction happens in the log shipper, on the node, before anything leaves it. The shipper config carries a `redact_fields` list — card numbers, email addresses, bearer tokens, the customer address block — and replaces each match with a stable hash, so you can still tell that two lines refer to the same value without learning what the value is.

Doing it at the shipper rather than in every application logger was a choice about where to put trust. Application-side redaction requires every service, in three languages, to remember every time; one new logging call in one new endpoint is enough to leak, and we would learn about it during an audit rather than during review. The shipper is one component, one config file, one reviewer.

The cost is that raw values exist briefly on disk in the container's stdout buffer before the shipper reads them. We accepted that: the node is inside the trust boundary, the window is seconds, and the alternative surface was far wider.

There is also a regex sweep for anything shaped like a card number regardless of field name. It fires on about one line a week and has caught two genuine mistakes.

All events pass through a `before_send` hook implemented in `libs/observability/scrub.py`, and `send_default_pii` is left off. The hook strips a denylist of header and body keys — authorization, cookie, and the fields carrying consignee address, contact phone and tax identifiers — and drops the query string from the request URL entirely rather than trying to filter it selectively. Selective query filtering was the first implementation and it leaked twice, both times because someone added a new parameter that carried an identifier and nobody thought to update the filter. Dropping the whole query string loses some debugging context and we decided that was the right trade: the path and method are retained, and anything genuinely needed for triage should be an explicit tag set by the code, not scraped from the URL. Local variables in stack frames are the remaining hazard, since a frame can hold a serialized shipment. The hook truncates frame locals above a size threshold and redacts values under keys matching the same denylist, which is imperfect — a PII value under an unexpected key still gets through. That residual risk is documented in the data-handling notes, and the tracker project is treated as a system holding customer data for retention purposes rather than as an ordinary tool.

End-to-end jobs set `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers` and cache that directory under a key derived from the exact resolved version of `@playwright/test`, not from the lockfile hash. The download is around four hundred megabytes of Chromium, Firefox and WebKit per job and was the largest single network cost in the pipeline. Keying on the package version rather than the whole lockfile means an unrelated dependency bump no longer forces a re-download, and unrelated bumps were the common case. The version has to be exact rather than a major or minor prefix: a driver upgrade running against browsers left from the previous minor produced teardown failures where the test body passed and the browser process still exited nonzero, which everyone triaged as flakiness. `npx playwright install --with-deps` still runs after the restore. It is a no-op when the binaries are present, and it is the only thing that installs the system libraries, which live outside the cached path and are therefore not covered by the key.

CI caches the pnpm content-addressable store rather than `node_modules`, and the key is `pnpm-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-node20`. A cold install of the console's dependencies cost about ninety seconds of a four-minute job and the lockfile changes roughly weekly, so the hit rate justifies the machinery. Two details were deliberate. Prefix fallback via restore-keys was removed after a partial restore left a store holding packages compiled against two different Node ABIs; a native binding loaded and then segfaulted inside the vitest worker, and for three days it read as flaky tests. Exact-match-only means a lockfile change costs a full install instead of a subtly wrong tree. The key also carries the Node major, because the store holds compiled output for `sharp` and `esbuild` and that output is not portable across an ABI boundary even when the lockfile is byte-identical. The store is safe to cache at all because it is content-addressed: a truncated or corrupt entry fails its integrity check on read rather than quietly producing different bytes. We accept the cold-install cost on lockfile churn as the price of that guarantee, and we do not cache anything that lacks an equivalent check.

Postmortems are due five working days after an incident is resolved, and only Sev1 and Sev2 require one. We picked five rather than the two we started with because two-day deadlines produced documents written from memory by an exhausted responder, and the genuinely useful detail — the dashboard nobody could find, the runbook step that was wrong — surfaced in conversation a week later regardless.

They are blameless in the strict sense: the document names systems and decisions, never people, and the review is facilitated by someone who was not on the incident. That second part matters more than the wording rule. When the responder runs their own review, the meeting becomes a defence, and everyone in the room can feel it.

Action items get an owner and a date or they do not go in the document at all. We deleted the recommendations section entirely after auditing a year of postmortems and finding that unassigned recommendations had a completion rate indistinguishable from zero.

Each preview namespace gets its own prefix in the shared staging bucket, named for the pull request, and a lifecycle rule expires everything under it after seven days. Before that, previews wrote to the same location as staging itself, and uploads from a branch under active development turned up in a colleague's manual test as unexplained documents; worse, a test that deleted files by prefix once removed uploads another environment was mid-test on. Separate buckets per preview were considered and rejected — bucket creation is slow, subject to account limits, and would need its own policy attached each time, which is a lot of machinery for isolating a few megabytes of test uploads. The prefix approach needs one credential scoped to that prefix and is created in the same step that creates the namespace. Expiry is the part that matters operationally: nothing cleans these up on merge, because a merge is not always the end of an environment, so the lifecycle rule is the only thing standing between us and unbounded growth, and it is set on the bucket rather than per prefix so a new preview cannot be created without inheriting it.

Proration rules in the legacy billing service are frozen. Any change to how a mid-cycle upgrade, downgrade, or cancellation is prorated requires the finance controller's sign-off before a line of code moves, and the answer has been no eleven times out of twelve. The rules encode about six years of accumulated special cases — annual plans bought on the thirty-first, customers on grandfathered currencies, one enterprise account with a contractual floor — and there is no oracle that tells you whether a change is correct, only whether it matches what the code did yesterday. A change that looks like a rounding fix restates revenue, which means restating reports that have already gone to the board. So the standing position is that behaviour is preserved bug-for-bug, and where the behaviour is genuinely wrong it is corrected by a manual credit note raised by finance rather than by touching the calculation. The single exception granted was a VAT rate change we were legally obliged to implement.

All public images are fetched through an in-region caching mirror rather than directly from the upstream registry. Two problems forced it. The first was rate limiting: anonymous pull quotas upstream are counted per source address, our whole cluster shares a handful of NAT addresses, and a large rollout could trip the limit and stall half the deploy behind pull errors that looked nothing like rate limiting. The second was egress cost — small per pull, and not small at all across a few thousand pod starts a day.

The mirror is a caching proxy, not a curated copy. It fetches on first request and holds what it has seen, so nobody has to remember to mirror a new dependency before using it, and nothing rots because a person forgot to sync it. We considered vendoring every third-party image into our own registry instead and rejected it: it creates a permanent curation burden that no team wanted to own.

Availability is the obvious risk, since the mirror is now a hard dependency of every cold pod start. It runs across three zones for that reason. A pleasant side effect is that its cache is the only complete list we have ever had of which external images we actually depend on.

A bot labels any pull request whose reviewable diff exceeds the threshold configured in `.github/pr-size.yml` as `max_changed_lines: 400`, with generated output excluded through a `paths_ignore` list covering `**/*.lock`, `**/openapi.gen.ts` and the migration snapshots. The number came from our own data: comments per hundred changed lines dropped sharply past about four hundred, and above a thousand the median review was a single approving sentence. That is not review, it is a signature. The label is a warning rather than a hard block, because occasionally a large mechanical rename genuinely is one change and splitting it would make it harder to read, not easier. What the label buys is a conversation before the review starts, and the standard answer is a stack of branches where each one is independently sensible. Authors were also asked to separate mechanical changes from behavioural ones into different commits at minimum, so a reviewer can skim the rename and concentrate on the twelve lines that matter.

Pull requests run a subset of the integration suite; the whole thing runs nightly. The subset is chosen by ownership rather than by timing — each service declares the integration cases that must pass before its code merges, and the rest, mostly cross-service journeys and long data migration checks, are deferred. Feedback on a pull request went from about forty minutes to nine, and the honest reason was behavioural: at forty minutes people stopped waiting, opened something else, and came back to a red build whose context they had lost. The nightly failure has an owner rota, one person a week, whose job is to triage before stand-up rather than to fix everything themselves. That role was the part we nearly skipped and the part that made the arrangement work; the first attempt had no owner and the nightly stayed red for eleven consecutive days before anyone looked at it.

Queue and cache state is not backed up, and that is a decision rather than an oversight. The broker holds work in flight and the cache holds derived data; both are reconstructible from Postgres, and a backup of either would be stale within seconds of being taken and would restore the system into a state that no longer matches its own database. Restoring a day-old queue would replay jobs that already ran, which for anything sending money or email is worse than losing them. What makes this safe is the rule that follows from it: any job that must survive total loss of the broker writes its intent as a row in Postgres before being enqueued, and the worker marks that row complete. Losing the broker then means replaying from the outstanding rows, which is idempotent by construction because the row is the identity. Jobs that do not follow the rule are allowed to exist but must be genuinely disposable — cache warms, thumbnail regeneration — and the review question for any new asynchronous work is which of the two categories it falls into. Getting that answer wrong is the only way this decision hurts.

Work is routed to one of three queues chosen by how long the job is allowed to take: `jobs.interactive` for anything a user is waiting on, `jobs.standard` for the ordinary asynchronous path, and `jobs.bulk` for backfills and exports. Each has its own worker deployment and its own scaling policy. Before the split there was a single queue and a single pool, and a nightly rate-card backfill enqueued about ninety thousand items that sat in front of the label-generation work customers were actively waiting for. Head-of-line blocking turned a batch job into a customer-visible outage twice before we accepted that priority within one queue was not going to save us — the workers were busy, and no priority scheme frees a busy worker. Routing is declared per job in the worker registry and validated at import: a job that declares a maximum duration above the interactive ceiling and also routes to `jobs.interactive` fails startup rather than being quietly accepted. The bulk pool is allowed to fall behind by design and its lag alert is measured in hours, while interactive lag alerts in seconds. That difference in expectations is the actual point of the split; the separate deployments are just how it is enforced.

Rate limiting for `api.halyard.io` is enforced in the edge gateway, not in per-service middleware. The filter chain and its descriptor mapping live in `ops/envoy/ratelimit.yaml`, and the services behind it carry no limiter code at all. Two things drove the move. Accounting was wrong when each service counted independently — a client fanning a workflow across the quotes and tracking services got effectively double its allowance, and support could not explain the discrepancy to customers. And the app-side limiter only rejected after the request had already occupied a worker, so a client hammering us still consumed the capacity we were trying to protect. Rejecting at the edge costs a fraction of a millisecond and never touches the upstream pool. The cost of this arrangement is that the gateway is now on the critical path for a policy decision, and gateway config changes go through a slower review than app code — a mistake there affects every endpoint at once. We considered that acceptable because the config is declarative and diffable, and `ops/bin/lint-ratelimit` validates the descriptor tree against the route table in CI so a typo'd descriptor cannot silently match nothing.

Refunds are issued as a credit note plus a separate payout, not as gateway reversals. A reversal is convenient — one call and the money returns the way it came — but it means different things at different acquirers depending on whether the original charge has settled, so the same operation is a void here and a refund there, with different timelines and different fee treatment, and support could never tell a customer when to expect their money. Credit notes made the accounting honest: the original invoice stands, the credit note references it, and the two net to what the customer actually paid, which is what the auditors want to see and what the tax treatment requires when the rate has moved between the charge and the refund. The cost is a slower path for the money and a support conversation about a document the customer did not ask for. We judged a predictable five days better than an unpredictable one to ten, and refund complaints fell by roughly half in the quarter after.

Registry retention keeps the last thirty builds per repository plus anything that has ever run in production, and deletes the rest after ninety days. Storage growth was the trigger — the registry had passed four terabytes, most of it pull-request builds from branches merged and deleted months earlier — but the final rule was shaped by rollback needs rather than by cost.

Thirty builds is about six weeks of merges for our busiest service and comfortably more than a year for the quietest. We considered a purely time-based rule and rejected it precisely because it would have left the quiet services with nothing to roll back to. The never-delete-if-deployed exception exists because we once garbage-collected an image that a long-running production deployment still referenced, and found out only when a node recycled and could not pull it.

Pull-request builds now go to a separate repository namespace with a ten-day sweep, which is what actually reclaimed the space. Keeping them out of the main repository also stopped them from crowding real releases out of the retention window.

Release branches are created from the release-candidate tag, never from whatever the trunk points at when the release manager runs the command. The step is `git switch -c release/2026.06 v2026.06.0-rc1`, and the runbook script refuses to proceed if that tag does not exist. We changed this after the June cut, where three pull requests merged in the eleven minutes between the go/no-go call and the branch creation, one of which shipped an unflagged change to invoice rounding. Cutting from the tag makes the release contents exactly the artefact QA signed off on, and it makes the difference between two releases a diff between two tags rather than an archaeology exercise across a moving branch. Hotfixes land on the release branch first and are cherry-picked forward the same day; the forward-port is a checklist item on the release issue because we have twice shipped a fix that quietly regressed in the following release. Release branches carry the same protection rules as the trunk and are deleted six months after the release leaves support.

Every process sets `SENTRY_RELEASE` to the short build SHA, injected at image build time from `git rev-parse --short HEAD`, and the deploy pipeline posts a deploy marker to the tracker as its last step. We tried using the human release version first and it was useless: hotfixes shipped under the same version string, so a regression introduced by a hotfix attributed to the original release and the "first seen in" field pointed at the wrong week. The SHA is unambiguous and maps directly to a diff. The deploy marker matters as much as the tag. Without it the tracker knows which build an error came from but not when that build reached which environment, so the regression detector could not tell a genuinely new issue from an old one arriving in a newly-scaled region. With markers, an issue that reopens on a specific deploy shows the deploy inline, and the median time from alert to identifying the offending PR dropped to something like a minute. The environment tag is set separately from `HALYARD_ENV`, and CI fails a deploy where the release tag is empty — an untagged build once produced three weeks of errors that could not be attributed to anything.

A proposal to adopt a task-graph runner with a hosted remote cache for the frontend was declined. The pitch was that task-level caching would let unaffected packages skip work entirely. In practice the console is one application plus a thin shared component package, so the graph has two useful nodes, and the modelled saving was under a minute on a pipeline that already finished in four. Against that we would have taken on a cache service to operate and secure, a new failure mode where a wrong key produces an artifact that is silently stale rather than a check that is visibly red, and a hard external dependency without which the pipeline cannot complete at all. The reviewers' position was that caching correctness bugs are the expensive class of bug precisely because they do not announce themselves, and that buying that exposure for sixty seconds is a bad trade. The decision was scoped to the repository's current shape and left explicitly open should the frontend ever split into genuinely independent packages with separate release cadences.

Request and response bodies are never logged, at any level, in any environment holding real data. This is a hard rule rather than a guideline, because the alternative is a case-by-case judgement made by whoever is writing an endpoint at the time, and that judgement gets made badly under deadline.

The reasoning is that bodies are where everything dangerous lives — full card details on the payment path, names and addresses on the customer path, tokens on the auth path — and field-level redaction cannot be trusted to keep pace with a schema that changes weekly. A field that is safe today acquires a new sibling next sprint and nobody remembers to update the rules.

What is allowed instead: the endpoint, the status, the timing, the payload size, and the identifiers that let you fetch the record from the system that is supposed to hold it. In practice that answers the question nine times out of ten, and for the tenth the correct move is to reproduce against a staging record rather than to go rummaging.

The single carve-out is local development, where bodies are logged freely and no real data exists.

CI retries a failing test once, and only for transport errors: `--reruns 1 --only-rerun 'ConnectionError|ReadTimeout'`. An assertion failure is never retried. Blanket reruns were in place for about a month and they are how a real bug hid from us — a race in the invoice numbering path failed roughly one run in six, the rerun swallowed it, and it surfaced in production as two invoices sharing a number on the same account. Restricting reruns to transport exceptions keeps genuinely environmental noise out of the way, mostly the container registry timing out during image pull, without letting a flaky assertion look green. Every rerun is counted and reported weekly, and a test that reruns more than twice in a week is treated as flaky and quarantined even though it is technically passing, because a repeated transport failure in one place is usually a missing timeout or a missing readiness check rather than bad luck. The rerun count has been a better flakiness signal than the failure count.

Jobs retry with exponential backoff and full jitter, capped at `max_retries = 5`, and any job that writes to the ledger must accept an `idempotency_key` that is derived from the triggering event rather than generated at execution time. Delivery is at-least-once and we stopped pretending otherwise: a worker that finishes its work and dies before acknowledging will have the same job redelivered, and that is not a rare event at our worker churn. Deriving the key from the event is the part people get wrong. A key generated inside the job body is different on every attempt and provides no protection at all, which is how a duplicate accrual reached a customer invoice and prompted the rule. Jitter was added after a downstream carrier API returned 503 for about ninety seconds and every failed job retried on the same synchronized schedule, hammering the recovering service in three sharp waves. The retry cap is low on purpose: five attempts across roughly ten minutes, then the dead-letter queue. Long retry ladders mostly serve to delay the moment a human learns something is broken, and we would rather surface it while the context is fresh.

`.github/workflows/review_reminder.yml` runs on cron `0 8,13 * * 1-5` in UTC and posts a single digest to the team channel listing open pull requests still waiting on a first review, oldest first, with the age in hours. It replaced a per-pull-request notification that direct-messaged a reviewer on every push. That version generated enough noise that most of the team muted it within a fortnight, which made it strictly worse than nothing because everyone assumed it was still working. The digest deliberately does not @-mention individuals: the message is addressed to the team, the team decides who picks it up, and pulling from the top is the norm. Twice a day was chosen over hourly because the schedule matches when people actually context-switch, once mid-morning and once after lunch, and the two runs straddle the working hours of both time zones on the team. Pull requests that already have a review in progress are filtered out, since the reminder is about the unattended queue and nothing else.

Percentage rollouts bucket on a hash of the account id combined with the flag key, not on a random draw per request. The evaluator computes `bucket = fnv1a(account_id + ":" + flag_key) % 100` and compares it against the configured percentage.

Two properties fall out of that, and both were requirements rather than accidents. First, an account gets a consistent answer for the lifetime of the rollout, so nobody watches a feature flicker between page loads — with a random draw, a 50% rollout means every single request is a coin flip and the resulting experience is incoherent. Second, mixing the flag key into the hash means the same accounts are not permanently in the first 10% of every rollout. Before we added the key, one unlucky set of customers was the canary for everything we shipped, and unsurprisingly they were the ones filing all the bug reports.

Where there is no account — unauthenticated traffic — the bucket falls back to a hash of the session id, and with neither the flag evaluates to its default. We explicitly do not bucket on IP address: shared corporate NAT put entire customer offices on the same side of every rollout.

Every service image ends with `USER 10001`, a numeric uid with no matching entry in `/etc/passwd`. Numeric rather than named because the Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot` check inspects the uid and cannot resolve a username — a named user passes the Dockerfile and then fails admission in a way that is genuinely confusing to debug.

We standardised on one uid across every service so that shared volumes and the sidecar log shipper need no per-service ownership rules. The application directory is chowned in the build stage, the runtime filesystem is mounted read-only, and the two services that need scratch space get an explicit `emptyDir` at `/tmp`.

The migration was not free. Three services were binding to port 80 and had to move to 8080, and one had been writing a cache into its own working directory, which surfaced as a crash loop the first time the read-only mount landed in staging. We did it anyway after a review pointed out that a container escape from any of our services would have started as root, and that the cost of being wrong about that once is enormously larger than a week of port changes.

Every schema change lands as at least two revisions in `alembic/versions/`, an expand and a contract, separated by at least one release. During a rolling deploy the old and new application versions run against a single database for several minutes, so a change that is atomic from the schema's point of view is not atomic from the application's. Renaming a column in one step breaks whichever half of the fleet has not rolled yet. The expand revision adds the new column nullable, application code is deployed writing both and reading the new one with a fallback, and only in a later release does the contract revision drop the old column, once no running version references it. The other half of the rule is that a revision may change the schema or move data but never both. Mixing them produces a migration whose duration depends on row count, which turns a deploy step with a predictable cost into one that can hold locks for minutes. Backfills are separate jobs for that reason.

A guard checks read-replica lag before the migration step runs and refuses to proceed above thirty seconds; the backfill runner checks the same figure between batches and slows itself down rather than stopping. Schema changes and bulk updates generate write-ahead log volume, the replicas serve every customer-facing reporting dashboard, and lag on those replicas turns directly into wrong numbers shown to customers with no indication that they are stale. That is the part that made this worth automating — a slow dashboard is visible and a subtly out-of-date one is not. The second reason is compounding: pushing more write volume at a database whose replicas are already behind makes the lag worse, so the naive behaviour of proceeding anyway is exactly backwards. A blocked deploy is a visible, cheap, recoverable inconvenience that someone will investigate within minutes. The threshold was set from the reporting refresh interval rather than picked for roundness, and it is reviewed whenever that interval changes.

`just seed` runs the factories in `seeds/factories.py` against an empty local database, deterministic under a fixed `SEED_RANDOM_STATE = 1337`. Populating local databases from a production dump was rejected on two grounds. The obvious one is that customer data on unmanaged laptops is a data-protection problem no amount of scrubbing fully answers, since the shapes survive scrubbing even when the values do not. The less obvious one, and the reason people stopped asking, is that generated data is reproducible: a bug report can carry a seed number and a factory name instead of a database dump, and everyone reproduces the same rows. The factories deliberately generate the awkward cases rather than the average ones — a tenant with zero shipments, a tenant with fifty thousand, a shipment whose destination is null because the carrier feed omitted it, a duplicate tracking number. Those are precisely the rows nobody had locally and everybody hit in production, and building them into the seed made a class of bug reproducible before release instead of after.

Our own service images are tagged with the short commit SHA and nothing else. No `latest`, no `staging`, no environment-named tags. A deploy is therefore a reference to exactly one build, and `kubectl get deploy -o wide` tells you which commit is running without having to ask anyone.

We used to publish an environment tag alongside the SHA and move it on promotion. It caused two distinct problems. Rollbacks became ambiguous, because the tag had already moved and nothing in the cluster could tell you what "the previous staging image" had been. Worse, a node that restarted a pod after the tag moved could quietly pull different content than its siblings, which produced a memorably bad afternoon where half the pods in one deployment were running code the other half were not.

Promotion is now a config change: the release job writes the same SHA tag that passed in staging into the production manifest. The artifact is built once and never rebuilt per environment, which also eliminated a class of "it worked in staging" failures caused by two supposedly identical builds not being identical at all.

Every service image builds on Debian slim. We standardised on it after two separate Alpine incidents that between them cost more engineering time than the image size ever saved.

The first was DNS. musl's resolver does not implement the search-domain retry behaviour glibc does, and `ingest-gateway` intermittently failed to resolve in-cluster service names under load, in a way that looked exactly like a network problem for three days. The second was performance: a Python service doing heavy JSON work ran roughly 30% slower against musl's allocator, and we burned most of a sprint profiling application code before anyone thought to suspect the libc.

The counter-argument was image size and it is real — the slim images are around 80 MB against Alpine's 8 MB. In practice the difference is invisible. Nodes cache layers, and pull time has never been on the critical path of a deploy for us. Trading 70 MB for a libc that behaves the way every upstream wheel and every vendor SDK expects was not a close call.

Services that genuinely need a small footprint build a static binary and copy it into a scratch stage instead. That path exists and two Go services use it.

The composition scanner runs on every image build, but only critical and high findings block a merge. Medium and low findings are collected into a weekly digest that the security rotation reads and mostly closes. This floor was set deliberately after a quarter in which the scanner produced several hundred findings and the team's response was to add blanket suppressions — the classic failure where a noisy gate trains people to disable the gate. Two additional rules make the floor honest. A finding is only downgraded with a written reason attached to the suppression, and every suppression carries an expiry no longer than one quarter, so nothing is permanently invisible. Second, findings in anything that parses untrusted input from the public API are exempt from the floor entirely and block regardless of the scanner's own severity rating, because the scanner scores in the abstract and we know our exposure better than it does. The rotation is explicitly allowed to say "not reachable from any code path we ship" and close a high finding, provided they say which code path they checked. We would rather have twenty findings a quarter that people actually read than four hundred that nobody does.

The protobuf and JSON schema definitions shared between services live in their own repository, `kestrel-schemas`, and are consumed as versioned releases rather than by path. Before that, each service vendored a copy and the copies diverged: two of them disagreed about whether a shipment identifier was a string or an integer, and the disagreement only surfaced when a message crossed between them in production. The repository is now the single source, tagged with semantic versions like `v2.7.0`, and CI runs `buf breaking --against '.git#tag=v2.7.0'` on every pull request so an incompatible field change cannot merge without an explicit major bump. Generated clients are published per language on tag — a Python wheel and a Go module — so consumers upgrade deliberately and the upgrade shows up as a lockfile diff. The cost is a two-step change: a schema pull request, then a bump in each consumer. That was accepted because the alternative made every consumer's build depend on whatever happened to be on the schema main branch at build time, which is a different failure and much harder to attribute. Field deprecation is by reserved tag number and a comment, never by deletion.

Every commit in the deploy repo must be signed. Branch protection has `require_signed_commits` enabled, and the settings sync app owns that flag so it cannot be switched off for a quick fix during an incident. The deploy repo holds the rendered manifests the cluster reconciles from, which means a write there is a production change with no further gate; an unsigned commit pushed with borrowed credentials would have applied within ninety seconds. Signing gives us a second factor bound to hardware — everyone uses a hardware key, and `git config --global commit.gpgsign true` with the key registered on the account is a line in the onboarding checklist. We deliberately did not extend the requirement to application repos. The setup cost per contributor is real, roughly six hours of support across the rollout week, and application repos already have review, CI, and a promotion step between merge and production. The bots that open manifest bumps sign with their own keys, rotated on the same quarterly schedule as the rest of that account.

Main takes squash merges only. We turned off merge commits and rebase-merge in the platform repo in March; the settings live in `.github/settings.yml` with `allow_merge_commit = false` and `allow_rebase_merge = false`, applied by the settings sync app so nobody can flip them back in the UI during a bad afternoon. The reason was bisect quality, not tidiness. Half the regressions we chased in Q4 landed inside a forty-commit merge, and `git bisect` kept stopping on intermediate commits that never built, so the operator had to skip, guess, and start over. One squashed commit per pull request means every point on the trunk is a state CI actually validated, and a revert is one commit rather than an argument about parent numbers. The cost is that intermediate authorship is lost, which reviewers of large refactors complained about loudly and fairly; we accepted it because the pull request is the durable record and the branch commits remain reachable through the API for ninety days. The squash message is generated from the pull request title plus the first paragraph of the body, which is why the ticket ID convention is load-bearing — a title without an `ENG-####` prefix produces a commit our changelog generator silently skips, and we have shipped two unannounced features that way. Vendored dependency bumps opened by the update bot are the one place the noise of a squash is irrelevant, and we left them on the same path rather than carving out an exception nobody would remember.

Staging is seeded from a scrubbed subset of production rather than from synthetic fixtures. The subset is roughly four percent of rows: the last ninety days of bookings plus everything they reference transitively, which preserves referential integrity without copying seven years of history. Scrubbing happens inside the extract job, never as a later pass, so unredacted data is never written anywhere outside the production account — `scrub_pii` rewrites email addresses into a deterministic `user+<id>@example.invalid` form, replaces names from a word list, nulls payment tokens and phone numbers, and shifts dates of birth by a per-row offset that preserves age bands. Determinism matters more than it sounds: a support engineer reproducing a customer's issue needs the same fake address for the same customer across two refreshes, and the earlier random rewrite made staging bug reports impossible to correlate. Synthetic fixtures were the original approach and were abandoned because they had no long tail — no shipment with eleven legs, no customer with an apostrophe in the name, none of the malformed addresses that cause most real bugs. The extract is the only process with read access into production from outside that account, and its role is narrowed to the tables it names explicitly.

All staging hostnames sit under a single wildcard certificate for `*.stg.kestrel.internal`, issued by the cluster's ACME issuer and stored as one secret the ingress references. The previous arrangement issued a certificate per hostname, which was tidy until preview environments arrived: every branch created a hostname, every hostname triggered an issuance, and we hit the authority's rate limit on a busy afternoon, leaving several previews serving an untrusted certificate and one engineer convinced the proxy was broken. A wildcard removes issuance from the critical path of creating an environment entirely. Resolution is split-horizon — the zone resolves only inside the network, which is also why a private issuer is acceptable here and would not be in production. The trade-off is blast radius: one private key covers everything in staging, so it is rotated on a shorter schedule than a production certificate would be and the secret is readable only by the ingress controller's service account.
