Production keeps per-hostname certificates from the public authority, deliberately, because there the failure modes of a shared key matter more than the convenience.

The staging reset moved from weekly to nightly, running at `0 3 * * *`: truncate the mutable tables, reload from the scrubbed extract, replay the baseline seed. Weekly resets meant that by Thursday the data carried six days of accumulated test debris — half-finished bookings, tenants created by an abandoned migration test, rows in states the application can no longer produce — and failures there were routinely unreproducible after a reset, which taught people to distrust staging failures in general. That is the expensive outcome: an environment nobody believes is worse than no environment. Nightly resets bound the drift to one day. Teams needing a fixture to survive the reset add it to `seeds/staging_baseline.sql`, which is reviewed like code and is a better home for a long-lived scenario than a row somebody created by hand and asked people not to touch. The reset announces itself in the engineering channel at start and finish, because the one real cost is losing an in-progress manual test at three in the morning, and the announcement plus a fixed hour turned out to be enough. Anyone needing longer-lived state uses an ephemeral namespace instead.

Staging runs on deliberately undersized infrastructure and performance testing was moved off it. The database there is a `db.r6g.large` against production's much larger class, application pods get a quarter of the CPU limit, and the cache is a single node rather than a replicated group. That is a cost decision and an appropriate one — staging exists to answer whether something works, not how fast. It became a problem when a load test run there produced throughput numbers that were used to build a capacity plan, and the plan was off by roughly five times in the wrong direction. Performance work now runs in a separate environment stood up from infrastructure code at production instance sizes, exercised, and destroyed the same day; it costs a few hundred a month because it exists for a few hours a week. The staging load test job was deleted rather than left in place with a warning comment, since a job that exists will eventually be trusted by someone who did not read the comment. What staging remains good for is the class of failure that scales down cleanly: missing indexes, N+1 queries, unbounded result sets, anything whose shape is visible at any size.

Staging talks to the payment provider's sandbox rather than to a local mock. The mock was maintained by us and drifted twice in a year, both times the same way: the provider added fields to a webhook and changed the ordering of two callbacks, our mock kept sending the old shape, and integration tests stayed green through a change that broke production within a day of shipping. A mock encodes our belief about someone else's system, and that belief goes stale silently. The sandbox has real signature verification, real idempotency-key behaviour, and real error responses including the rate-limit path the mock never modelled at all, which is where two of our worst bugs lived. It also has costs we accepted: it is slower, occasionally unavailable at night, and enforces limits that lengthen a full suite run, so contract tests retry with backoff and the suite is not allowed to fail the build on a sandbox timeout — only on a sandbox rejection. Its credentials are sandbox-scoped and are the only third-party credentials staging holds. Unit tests still use fakes; the distinction is that a fake standing in for a dependency inside one test is not a claim about the outside world.

Staging was moved into its own account and network after a job running there wrote messages onto a production queue. The two environments had been peered so staging could read from a production replica during seeding, and a service whose `broker_url` fell back to the value baked into its packaged defaults did the rest; the messages turned out harmless, and their being harmless was luck rather than design. Peering was removed. Staging now reaches nothing in production: seeding goes through an export written by a production-side job into a shared bucket, pull rather than push, and the bucket policy grants staging read on exactly one prefix. Egress from staging is restricted to third-party sandbox endpoints on an allowlist. The immediate cost was losing the ability to point a staging service at a production replica while debugging, which people did more often than anyone admitted, and the replacement is a documented process for exporting one customer's records into staging with approval. The general rule that came out of it is that environment isolation cannot depend on configuration being correct, because configuration is exactly what is wrong during an incident.

Tax is quoted by the vendor API and cached locally for twenty-four hours in `tax_quote_cache`, keyed on `(jurisdiction, product_code, effective_date)`. We stopped maintaining rates in-house after a Norwegian VAT change that we learned about from a customer complaint. The cache exists because the vendor is a hard dependency in the invoice path and their published availability is two nines; during a forty-minute outage last year the cache served every quote we needed and nobody noticed. Rates change on legislative timelines, so a day-old quote is correct essentially always, and putting the effective date in the key means a scheduled change is not masked by a stale entry the morning it takes effect. The rule we wrote down is that a cache miss during a vendor outage fails the invoice rather than guessing: an invoice with a wrong tax line is a legal problem, a late invoice is an operational one. Each quote is stored with the vendor's response identifier so an audit can be traced back to the exact calculation they returned.

Test data comes from `tests/factories.py` rather than YAML fixture files. A case that needs an overdue invoice writes `make_invoice(status="past_due", days_overdue=45)` and gets a coherent object graph — customer, subscription, tax jurisdiction — with every unnamed field filled in with a valid default. The fixture files it replaced had grown to roughly eighteen hundred lines shared by sixty tests, so nobody could change one without breaking something unrelated; people added a near-copy instead, and we ended up with four subtly different "standard customer" records, none of which matched what production actually stored. Factories also make a test readable: the two fields that matter to the assertion are the two fields in the call, and anything unnamed is by definition irrelevant to that case. Defaults live in one place, so when the subscription model gained a required billing-cycle column we changed one line instead of eighteen hundred. The migration took two weeks of background effort and we deleted the fixture directory outright rather than let both styles coexist.

The nightly backup starts at 01:15, moved from 02:00, because it was overlapping the warehouse extract. The extract holds long read transactions across the largest tables, and running it concurrently with a base backup pushed both past their windows: the backup finished after the morning traffic ramp on three occasions and the extract missed its delivery time twice. The schedule is now `15 1 * * *` for the base backup and 03:30 for the extract, with a documented ninety-minute gap that comfortably exceeds the longest observed backup. Neither job may be rescheduled by the team that owns it without a note in the shared night schedule; that file is the only place the whole night is visible, and the incident happened because two locally reasonable decisions were made independently. Both jobs emit start and finish times as metrics, and an alert fires when the gap between them drops below thirty minutes, which catches drift before it becomes an overlap. Growth is the thing to watch: backup duration has tracked database size, and at the current rate the gap closes in about eighteen months.

Adopting Bazel was proposed and declined. The pitch was correct about the problems — builds that redo work, test selection that runs everything, container images assembled by shell — and the counterargument was about proportion. The engineering group is fourteen people across two languages, both with adequate native build tooling, and the estimated migration was a full quarter of one person plus a long tail of everyone else relearning how to run a test. Remote caching, where most of the benefit lives, would have meant operating a cache service ourselves, and the majority of the wall-clock win the proposal projected was already available from content-keyed dependency caching in CI, which took a day to implement and delivered it. The decision was recorded together with the conditions that would reverse it: a third language, a build graph deep enough that correct incremental test selection stops being expressible in the existing tooling, or a team large enough that build engineering is somebody's actual job. None of those was true then and none has become true since. The proposal document is a good one and is worth rereading rather than rewriting if the subject returns.

Image scanning runs as a build step rather than a nightly report, and a critical finding fails the build. We moved it into the build after a quarter of nightly reports that everyone had learned to skim: the mean age of an unaddressed critical finding was 41 days.

High and medium findings are recorded and do not block. Only critical does. Exceptions live in a checked-in `.trivyignore` next to the Dockerfile, and each line requires a ticket reference and an expiry date in the comment beside it. Making the exception file a reviewed artifact in the service's own repository was the entire point — the previous mechanism was a shared allowlist inside the scanner's own configuration that nobody read and that contained entries older than the team.

The predictable objection was that this blocks releases on vulnerabilities in transitive OS packages we cannot fix ourselves. That happens perhaps once a quarter, and the escape hatch — add an ignore line with a ticket, ship, fix within the sprint — takes about four minutes. We judged four minutes a quarter better than a scanner nobody looked at.

We dropped the fourth dunning attempt. The retry ladder was day one, day three, day seven, day fourteen; the fourth attempt recovered three-tenths of a percent of the invoices that reached it, and every attempt against an already-declined card counts against our authorisation rate with the acquirer, who had raised it with us twice. Three attempts recover essentially everything recoverable — money that arrives after day seven arrives because a human read the email, not because the card started working. The fourth attempt was also the largest single source of angry support tickets, from customers who had already cancelled and then watched us try to charge them a fortnight later. What replaced it is one final notice at day fourteen carrying a payment link and no automatic charge, which recovers roughly the same fraction with none of the complaints. Finance agreed on the condition that accounts still move to suspended on the previous schedule, so nothing changed on the revenue recognition side.

The payment gateway key is rotated quarterly using the provider's two-active-key window: introduce the new key, watch their dashboard until all traffic is signed with it, then retire the old one after the seven-day overlap. This replaced an emergency-shaped process where someone swapped the key at two in the morning and the team held its breath through the following settlement run. The overlap is why it is boring now — nothing has to happen simultaneously, and a mistake is caught while the previous key still works. We rotate on a schedule rather than only on suspicion, because a rotation that is never rehearsed is not a control, it is a hope; the first drill took most of a day and the most recent took forty minutes. Finance gets a week's notice, because a rotation shows up as a brief flat spot in their live authorisation graph and they opened an incident about it once.

The legacy billing database stays on MySQL 5.7 until the service is decommissioned. We costed the 8.0 upgrade twice and hit the same wall both times: the schema and roughly two hundred queries were written against a permissive `sql_mode`, and 8.0 turns on `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` by default, so a meaningful share of the reporting queries stop returning rows and start returning errors. Fixing them means reconstructing the intent of queries whose authors left the company years ago, inside a service that has a scheduled end. We bought extended support instead, which costs less per year than the engineering time and delivers the security patches that were the real reason to move. The conditions were written down alongside the decision, because an exception without conditions becomes a permanent state: the instance is reachable only from the billing service and its read replica, backups are restore-tested monthly rather than the usual quarterly, and any new data requirement is served from elsewhere rather than by adding a table here. Two requests have been refused on that last clause. If decommission slips past the end of the support contract we revisit, and that is a date tracked on the roadmap rather than an intention.

`services/billing-legacy/` is frozen to security patches and legally mandated changes. A CI check named `freeze_guard` fails any pull request touching that path unless it carries the `freeze-exception` label, which only the billing tech lead and the security team can apply. The freeze is not because the code is bad, though it is; it is because every hour spent improving something with a scheduled end is an hour not spent on its replacement, and because each change carries outsized regression risk in a system whose failure mode is charging a customer the wrong amount. Twenty-two exceptions have been granted in nine months: fourteen dependency patches, five tax and regulatory changes, and three production defects that were losing money. Feature requests that would once have landed here are refused with a note pointing at the successor system, which has turned out to be an effective forcing function on the teams still asking for them. The freeze covers code only — index changes, capacity work, and monitoring are unaffected and have needed regular attention.

The quotes service was left on its own hand-written, numbered SQL migration files instead of being folded into the shared tooling. It predates that tooling, owns a separate database that nothing else reads, and its schema changes about twice a year. The port was estimated at two weeks of work and would have bought consistency and nothing else — no new safety property, no reduced operational burden, no shared code path that anyone would exercise often enough to keep working. The team's position was that consistency is a real value but not a free one, and paying two weeks for it against a service with a retirement date on the roadmap is a bad trade. What did get written down were the two properties that actually matter and that the shared tooling happens to provide: changes go through review like any other code, and they apply in a deploy step ahead of the application rather than from the service itself. Those were made explicit for the quotes service in its own runbook. The mechanism was left alone, and the sunset is tied to the service's retirement rather than to a tooling cleanup that would never be prioritised on its own.

The tracker runs on a fixed monthly event budget, and we chose to keep the budget flat and cut noise rather than raise the plan every time we hit the ceiling. When the quota is exhausted the vendor drops events for the rest of the period, which is the worst possible failure mode — you lose visibility precisely when something is going wrong, since the thing that burned the quota is usually the thing you need to see. So the guard is on the way in, not at the ceiling: a spend alert fires at seventy percent of budget with the top event producers attached, and whoever is on observability rotation that week is expected to bring the biggest contributor down. In practice that has always been the right call. Every time we have looked, the top producer was a single high-volume issue that nobody was going to fix and that carried no information after the first hundred occurrences. Raising the plan would have paid to store more copies of it. The one time we did increase the budget, it was because service count had genuinely grown and the per-service baseline was reasonable; that is the test we apply now.

We retired the bot that merged trunk into every open feature branch overnight. It was introduced to keep branches close to the mainline, and for a while it did, but the cost showed up as churn: authors arrived each morning to a branch they had not touched, carrying a merge they had not reviewed, and in two cases the bot resolved a conflict in favour of the mainline and silently undid a colleague's fix. The deeper problem was that it made staleness invisible. A branch that would have loudly conflicted after a week instead accumulated a dozen automated merges and looked healthy right up to the point where its behaviour no longer matched anyone's mental model of it. Now branches go stale honestly, and the merge queue refuses anything more than fifty commits behind, which pushes people to either finish the work or abandon it. Long-lived branches dropped from about fifteen open at any time to four, and each of the survivors has an owner who can say what state it is in. Nobody has asked for the bot back.

`nightly_reconcile` used to page and no longer does. It walks yesterday's ledger entries against the settlement file from the bank and fails perhaps twice a month, almost always because the file arrived late or arrived truncated. Nobody has ever fixed one of those at 04:00 — the fix is to wait for the bank to re-send, or to re-run once the file lands.

So we demoted it. The job writes its failure into the platform ticket queue with the run id and the offending batch, and the morning responder picks it up in working hours. The only path back to the pager is an age check: if reconciliation has not succeeded for thirty-six hours, that is a Sev2, because at that point we are genuinely blind to settlement drift and month-end is at risk.

The general principle we took from this and applied to four other batch jobs: something that fails predictably and cannot be fixed while half-asleep does not deserve a pager. Alert on the deadline being missed, not on the individual failure.

The payment gateway is replayed from recorded interactions in integration. Cassettes live under `tests/cassettes/` and the client runs with `record_mode = none`, so an unmatched request fails loudly instead of quietly reaching the network from a build agent. We tried a hand-written fake first and it drifted within a quarter: the fake happily accepted a field the real API had begun rejecting, and the mismatch reached production as a wave of declined authorisations on one card brand. Recordings are captured against the gateway sandbox by an on-demand job, and re-recording arrives as a reviewable diff, which means an upstream API change shows up as a change to a file rather than as a surprise at deploy time. The known weakness is that a cassette is a snapshot and can rot silently, so a weekly contract check replays a small set of requests against the live sandbox and opens a ticket when a response shape has moved; it has caught two changes so far, one of them a new required field on refunds. Cassettes are scrubbed of card numbers and tokens at record time by a filter configured in the test harness, and the scrubber is itself tested, because the first version missed the field holding the network token.

A checkout latency spike was diagnosed as slow queries for most of an afternoon before anyone looked at the pooler. Tracing showed database spans of four to nine seconds on `booking-api`, and the query text in those spans was a primary-key lookup that has never taken longer than two milliseconds. The spans were measuring connection acquisition and execution together. The actual cause was an ad-hoc migration script left running in a psql session with an open transaction; it held server connections in the dispatch pool, and every checkout request queued behind it. Two fixes came out of it. First, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 30s` on the application roles, so an abandoned session cannot hold a server connection indefinitely. Second, and more important, the client library now records `db_pool_acquire_seconds` as a histogram separate from query duration, and the dashboard shows them side by side. The distinction matters because the two have opposite remedies: slow queries want an index or a rewrite, while acquisition waits want a bigger pool, a shorter transaction, or the removal of whatever is squatting. The runbook now opens with checking pool waiting counts before reading a single query plan.

We moved the primary on-call shift boundary from Monday 09:00 to Wednesday 10:00 in March, after two quarters of complaints that shifts started with a weekend hangover. A Monday start meant whoever picked up the pager inherited whatever the weekend had broken plus the Monday deploy surge, and the handoff happened during the busiest hour of the week. Wednesday-to-Wednesday puts the boundary in the calmest part of the cycle: releases have soaked for two days, and the outgoing responder is still around for two working days to answer questions about anything they left half-fixed.

Shift length stayed at seven days. We tried five-day shifts for one quarter and abandoned them — the rotation only has nine people, so five-day shifts meant someone was on call roughly every seven weeks and paid two boundaries' worth of context loss instead of one. Longer shifts amortise the ramp-up cost, and the ramp-up cost is most of the cost.

The schedule lives in `rotations/platform_primary.yaml` and is synced to the paging vendor by a nightly job; edits go through review like any other config, mostly so that swaps leave a record. Swaps themselves are self-serve and need no approval — we found approval gates just made people work shifts while sick.

We hold the pull-request pipeline to fifteen minutes and cut whatever it takes to stay there. Three things went: contract tests against downstream services moved to the merge queue, coverage upload became fire-and-forget instead of a gate, and the browser suite shrank from nineteen scripted journeys to three that represent money moving. The number is arbitrary and the reasoning is not — past roughly a quarter of an hour people context-switch, and the cost of a slow pipeline is paid in half-finished reviews and stale branches rather than in compute spend. Enforcement is a weekly report of median and ninety-fifth-percentile duration, and any step that pushes the median over budget is optimised or moved to a later stage by whoever added it. It has held for seven months. The steady pressure comes from new services adding their own jobs, and the answer there has been to run each job only when its own directory changed.

The billing reconciliation job runs at `0 3 * * *` UTC. The hour is not arbitrary: the gateway drops its settlement file at 02:15 UTC and it has landed complete by about 02:40 on the worst day we have measured. The original schedule ran at midnight and produced phantom mismatches for every transaction settled after the file we happened to have — a hundred-odd rows a night that someone eyeballed and dismissed, which trained everyone to dismiss the report without reading it. Running after the drop means a mismatch is a real mismatch, the report is usually empty, and a non-empty one gets attention. The job writes into `billing_reconcile` and pages the finance-engineering rota only when the unmatched total crosses a threshold denominated in money rather than in row count, because one large unmatched charge matters and forty small rounding differences do not. It is also why the nightly maintenance window moved to 04:00; two jobs contending for the same tables were producing lock timeouts about once a fortnight.

A proposal to run one pooler instance per large tenant, routing by a header at the gateway, was turned down. The motivation was real: three tenants account for roughly sixty percent of query volume, and a batch import from any of them visibly degrades everyone else's p99 for a few minutes. The objection was that sharding the pooler treats a scheduling problem as a topology problem. Each shard would need its own configuration, health checks, alert routes and capacity headroom, and the headroom is the expensive part — the sum of per-tenant peaks is far larger than the observed aggregate peak, so we would buy fewer usable connections in total while spending more to operate them. Failover also gets worse, because a tenant whose pooler is down has no fallback, whereas today any client can use any pooler node. What we did instead was cap concurrent batch imports per tenant at the API layer and give bulk endpoints their own lower-priority worker pool, which removed the observed symptom in an afternoon. The proposal is worth reopening only if a single tenant's steady-state load, not its bursts, exceeds what one primary can serve, at which point the conversation is about separate databases rather than separate poolers.

We defined three severities and wrote them down in `docs/incident-severity.md` after a long argument about whether a degraded search index counted as "an outage". Sev1 means money stops moving or customer data is at risk — checkout returning errors, the ledger falling behind settlement. Sev2 means a customer-visible feature is broken while the core path still works. Sev3 is internal-only or cosmetic and never wakes anyone.

The rule we settled on is that anyone can declare, and declaring is never wrong. Whoever notices names a severity out loud in the incident channel, and it is the responder's job to downgrade later if it turns out smaller than it looked. We chose that direction deliberately: the failure mode we had been living with was engineers sitting on a suspicion for twenty minutes because they did not feel senior enough to call it. Over-declaring costs a few minutes of attention. Under-declaring cost us a four-hour partial outage in January that three people had privately noticed and none had named.

Severity is also the only input to the customer-communications trigger — Sev1 and Sev2 open a status page entry within fifteen minutes, Sev3 never does. Keeping that mapping mechanical ended the recurring debate about whether a given incident was "worth" a public note.

A throttled request returns 429 with a stable, documented envelope: `Retry-After` in whole seconds, plus `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset`, and a JSON body whose error code is `rate_limited`. The header set follows the IETF draft naming rather than the `X-`-prefixed variant we shipped first; we took the one-time breaking change during the v2 API cut because two customers had already written parsers against the draft names from other vendors. The important decision was including `Retry-After` on every throttle, not just some. Our own SDKs back off using it, and before it was mandatory the SDK fell through to a fixed one-second retry, which turned a brief throttle into a synchronized retry wave from every client at once. The headers are also emitted on successful responses, which was debated — it costs three header lines on every request in the fleet — and adopted because it lets integrators see themselves approaching a limit instead of discovering it as an outage. The body deliberately does not say which limit was hit or how much of it remains beyond the header values; that detail leaks account configuration to anyone holding a key.

The shift handoff document is generated, not written. `make oncall-handoff` pulls everything from the last seven days — resolved incidents with their severity, alerts that fired more than twice, open tickets tagged `oncall`, and every active alert silence with its expiry — and drops a markdown file into the shared drive. The outgoing responder adds prose at the top and that is the whole ritual.

We built it because the handwritten version had rotted. People wrote three bullet points at the end of a tiring week and reliably forgot the silence they had set on Tuesday, which is how a muted alert on the dispatch queue survived eleven days. Silences whose expiry falls past the shift boundary now appear in bold in the generated section, and the outgoing responder has to either extend them explicitly or let them lapse.

The handoff itself stayed a fifteen-minute call rather than a document drop. We tried async-only for a quarter and it did not stick — the genuinely useful content turned out to be the things nobody would ever write down, like which customer had been emailing about latency all week, or which dashboard was lying.

TLS for database traffic terminates at the pooler process itself rather than at a sidecar proxy in front of it. The sidecar arrangement worked but replaced every client address in the pooler's logs with the loopback address of the proxy, which made authentication-failure triage nearly impossible — during a credential rotation we could see that something was failing to connect and had no way to tell which deployment it was. Terminating in the pooler restores the source address in its log lines and in its own connection listings. Certificates come from the internal certificate authority with short lifetimes and are rotated by the node agent; the pooler reloads them without dropping established connections, which was confirmed during the last rotation. Clients are configured to require full verification of the server name rather than merely encrypting, because encryption without verification protects against a passive observer and not against the misrouting we actually worry about in a shared cluster. The hop from pooler to Postgres is encrypted too despite both sitting in the same subnet; that hop carries every credential and query in the system, the auditors asked, and the measured cost was under a millisecond.

The trace identifier of the request that enqueued a job travels with the job and is adopted by the worker as its parent, so a single trace spans the synchronous request and the asynchronous work it triggered. This was not free — it required the enqueue path to capture the current context and the worker's startup to restore it before any application code runs — and it repaid the effort within the first month. The problem it solved was that support tickets described a user-visible symptom, the request that caused it had returned successfully, and the actual failure happened ninety seconds later in a worker with no link back. Investigations routinely involved guessing at a time window and grepping. Now the identifier appears in the customer-facing correlation reference too, so a support ticket carries the string that finds both halves. The rule extends to jobs that enqueue other jobs, which is where it gets genuinely valuable: a fan-out that spawns two hundred children shows them under one parent, and a partial failure is immediately visible as a shape rather than as two hundred unrelated errors that someone has to notice are related.

An issue that nobody assigns within fourteen days is automatically marked resolved, and it reopens the moment it recurs. This was introduced when the unresolved backlog passed three thousand issues, at which point the list had stopped functioning as a work queue and had become a monument. Nobody scrolled it, nobody triaged it, and new issues were indistinguishable from four-year-old ones. The auto-resolve rule is not a claim that the issue was fixed. It is an admission that we are not going to act on it, made explicit and reversible. If the underlying problem is still happening, the next occurrence reopens the issue with its full history intact and it re-enters triage — so the rule preferentially clears out things that stopped happening on their own, which is exactly the population we wanted gone. The visible effect was that the backlog fell by roughly ninety percent in a month and stayed low, and that reopened issues became a meaningful signal in their own right: an issue that has reopened three times is one we keep deciding not to fix and keeps insisting otherwise. Those get escalated in the weekly review rather than resolved again.

The vault cluster is sealed at rest and the master key is split five ways with `unseal_threshold = 3`. Shares are held by two SREs, the CTO, the head of finance engineering, and one sealed envelope in the office safe. Putting a share outside the engineering org was deliberate: a compromise of engineering accounts alone should not be enough to reconstitute the key. Auto-unseal backed by the cloud KMS was evaluated and rejected, because it collapses the whole ceremony into whoever holds one IAM role, which is exactly the single point we were trying to avoid; the price we accepted is a manual `vault operator unseal` round on any cold start. The last cold start took nineteen minutes, most of it spent finding the third holder on a Friday evening, so the rota now guarantees two reachable holders at any hour. Shares were re-keyed once, when a holder left the company, and the procedure for that lives with the disaster recovery documents rather than in the platform repo.

The retry-budget logic used by every outbound HTTP client is vendored into `libs/vendor/retry_budget.py` rather than installed from the registry. The upstream package is about 130 lines, has a single maintainer, and had gone eleven months without a release when we needed a fix for its clock handling. Copying it cost an afternoon; carrying it as a dependency would have meant either pinning to a version with a known bug or maintaining a fork on a private index, which we have no infrastructure for. The vendored file keeps its original license header and a provenance comment naming the upstream project and the commit it was taken from, and `tools/check_vendor_drift.py` fails CI if the header is stripped. We also copied the upstream test suite into `libs/vendor/tests/` unchanged, so a future re-sync has a baseline. This is deliberately not a general pattern. The bar we set was: under roughly 200 lines, no transitive dependencies of its own, no security-sensitive parsing, and a demonstrated need to modify it. Two later proposals to vendor larger helpers were rejected on the parsing clause alone — anything that reads untrusted bytes should be getting upstream security fixes automatically, not through us noticing.

WAL archive retention is fourteen days, raised from seven after a billing rounding bug went unnoticed for nine. The retention window is not a storage decision, it is a statement about how long we might take to discover that data was corrupted rather than lost — a lost cluster is obvious within minutes, but a bad migration that writes wrong values is discovered when someone reconciles a month-end close. Seven days did not cover the gap between the deploy and the reconciliation; fourteen covers every close we have. The setting lives in the backup tool's configuration as `retention_policy = "RECOVERY WINDOW OF 14 DAYS"`, with the base backup schedule sized so a full backup always exists at the far edge of that window, since a WAL archive with no base backup preceding it restores nothing. Archive segments go to the same bucket as the base backups but under a separate prefix with its own lifecycle rule, so a cost-driven change to one cannot silently shorten the other — that coupling is exactly how a retention window gets quietly reduced. Going beyond fourteen was priced and is affordable; it was not adopted because no discovery scenario we could describe needed it.

We built the flag service rather than adopting a vendor, and the decision was much closer than the outcome makes it look.

The vendor offering was better on every dimension visible on the day: a nicer console, real targeting rules, audit trails, SDKs in every language we use. What we could not get comfortable with was the dependency shape. Flags sit on the payment path, and the evaluation model on offer at the time either called out to their edge or relied on a streaming connection whose failure behaviour we could not characterise to our own satisfaction. Adding a third-party availability dependency to checkout in order to save a few weeks of engineering was the wrong trade for a company whose entire product is moving money reliably.

The secondary reason was data. Targeting rules meant sending account identifiers and attributes to a third party, which converts a build-versus-buy question into a vendor review, a data processing agreement, and a conversation with legal.

The cost is real and ongoing: we own a console nobody loves, our targeting is cruder than theirs, and about one engineer-week a quarter goes into maintenance. Two years on, that still looks like the right price.

A migration to distroless runtime images was proposed and turned down. The security argument was sound — no shell, no package manager, a much smaller surface if something does get remote execution — and we did not dispute any of it.

What we weighed against it was debugging. Our incident practice leans heavily on being able to open a shell inside a running container and look: check whether the config file actually contains what the config map claims, run a resolver query, list open sockets. Ephemeral debug containers technically solve this, but they were awkward on our cluster version, and the realistic outcome of the migration was that the median responder at 02:00 would lose a familiar tool in exchange for mitigating a threat that has never actually materialised for us.

The compromise was to strip the package manager from the runtime stage while keeping a shell and a handful of diagnostic binaries. That removes the thing an attacker most wants — the ability to install more tooling — without removing the thing our own people use.

Worth revisiting once ephemeral debug containers are boring and everyone has used them at least once outside an incident.

The logging backend moved from a self-managed Elasticsearch cluster to a label-indexed store. Cost was the headline — indexing every field of every line meant the index was consistently larger than the data it described — but operational load is what actually decided it. The cluster needed a person watching it. Shard rebalancing during a node replacement could occupy most of a day, and twice a hot node filled during a traffic spike and started rejecting writes.

The replacement indexes only labels and keeps line bodies compressed in object storage. Queries that filter by service and time and then grep are fast; queries asking for an arbitrary substring across everything are slow, sometimes painfully so. We took that trade after auditing our saved queries and finding that nearly all of them already began with a service and a time range.

The discipline it imposed is label cardinality. Putting a request id or a customer id into a label looks harmless and destroys the index, so labels are restricted to a fixed set and adding one requires review. Two teams learned that the hard way in the first month; the third had a guardrail because of them.

Alerting was rewritten around symptoms in the autumn. The old rule set had ninety-one alerts, most of them thresholds on individual hosts — disk above 85%, load average, a single pod restarting — and roughly a fifth of everything that reached the pager needed no action at all. We deleted all of them and replaced them with two burn-rate alerts per user-facing service, computed against that service's published SLO. `burn_rate_fast` fires when the last hour is spending error budget fourteen times faster than sustainable; `burn_rate_slow` needs six hours of two-times burn before it says anything.

The reasoning is that nobody is paid to care about a hot disk at 03:00 unless a customer can feel it. Capacity problems that are not yet hurting anyone became dashboard panels and a weekly review. Node-level conditions still flow through the same pipeline and still open tickets; they just do not ring.

Page volume dropped from about eleven a week to three. The cost we knowingly accepted is a longer time to first signal on slow-burning infrastructure problems — a disk that fills over nine days now gets noticed by a human reading a graph rather than by an alert. That was worth paying for a rotation that trusts the pager again.

`uv.lock` is regenerated on a schedule rather than opportunistically. A Monday-morning job runs `uv lock --upgrade`, opens one PR against main, and assigns it to whoever is on platform rotation that week. Before that, every feature branch that touched dependencies re-resolved the whole tree, so unrelated transitive bumps rode into product PRs and the blame for a broken build landed on the wrong author. Lockfile merge conflicts are never hand-resolved. `.gitattributes` marks the file with `uv.lock -diff` so reviewers stop trying, and the documented fix is to take main's copy and re-run `uv lock` — hand-edited lock entries produced two incidents where the hashes no longer matched the resolved versions and the container built from a cached layer instead of failing. The rotation owner is expected to read the diff, not just green-tick it: majors and anything touching the TLS or serialization stack get split into their own PR with a manual smoke deploy to staging. Everything else merges once the matrix is green. The weekly cadence was chosen because it matches the release train; a lock refreshed on Monday has four days of staging soak before Friday's cut.

A single key hitting its ceiling is not an incident and does not page. It is expected behaviour, it usually means an integrator wrote a loop without backoff, and it goes to the support queue with a link to the account. What pages is a rise in the fleet-wide rejection ratio across many distinct keys at once, because that pattern almost never means many customers simultaneously misbehaved — it means we shipped a config change that broadened a descriptor, or a plan mapping regressed, or the backend is misreporting. The distinction was drawn after a quarter in which on-call was woken four times for a single batch integrator and once, too late, for a genuine misconfiguration that had been throttling a whole tier for two hours while the noise from the batch job hid it. The dashboard carries the per-key detail for whoever is investigating; the alert carries only the cross-key signal. We deliberately did not build a threshold per customer. Tracking every key's normal rejection rate would produce a maintenance burden proportional to the customer count, and the one question the alert needs to answer is whether the change is ours.

Read traffic goes through its own pooler database entry, `bookings_ro`, pointed at the replica endpoint, rather than through a single pool that load-balances between primary and standby. The reason is that replica lag is a correctness property the application has to opt into, not something a connection layer should decide silently. A shared pool would have made read-after-write behaviour depend on which server connection a request happened to land on, and we had already spent a week chasing a booking confirmation that intermittently showed stale state. Services that can tolerate lag configure a second DSN and use it deliberately; everything else keeps using the primary entry. The `bookings_ro` entry runs in transaction mode with `default_pool_size = 25`, larger than the primary pool because read transactions are longer and cheaper, and it has its own `server_lifetime` so connections drain onto a new standby within minutes of a failover. The pooler does not fail read traffic back to the primary automatically; if the standby is unreachable the reads error, which is loud, and we preferred loud to a silent write-load surprise on the primary during an incident. Lag above thirty seconds pages, because past that the opt-in contract is no longer being honoured.
